speechtext: Do not forget Collingwood.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Well, last but not least, Collingwood. Is this waterway going to affect our railroad system that we are constantly paying to keep going? Is the effect going to be such that there will be increased taxation to pay for the lack of freight on our railroads? I just wonder how many men in the House of Commons have given this matter a great deal of thought, outside of visualizing the continual stream of traffic up the St. Lawrence river, in to Toronto, through lake Erie, up the St. Clair river, in to Owen Sound, and every town booming on account of this seaway. I really think most of them have not given the matter thorough study, having regard to what we are not doing in other parts of Canada.
To me, this project is not worth anything running on its own. What freight are we actually going to ship to Europe outside of our wheat? Our manufactured products? The Europeans are down on their hands and knees now trying to ship us their manufactured products so they can buy our wheat. We all seem to think the St. Lawrence waterway is going to make all the manufacturing concerns of Ontario and Quebec boom, that they will load up these boats with goods, send them: down the river and over to buyers, who cannot afford to pay for our products. The next thing will be that you will find this government wanting to lend money that they know they will never get back. We are doing that with regard to our wheat today. They will say: Buy our electric trains made in Owen Sound and Collingwood. We will lend you the money to buy them with. We have the deep waterway. We must use it. We spent the public's money on it. Two hundred and fifty million dollars? Watch it when it is

St. Lawrence Waterway finished. I will go on record tonight as saying that it will cost closer to $400 million before it is finished in six, eight or ten years time. This country has only so much money to spend. The taxpayers can afford only so much.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: They are gouged now.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: They are going to be gouged some more.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Can they afford this expenditure? I am not trying to take some political stand on this subject. I am not trying to catch votes. I am trying to talk facts. Can the taxpayers of Canada, with a population of 14 million, afford this enterprise at the present time? Are there not many more essential things that we need?
I know western Canada. I know every part of it. I know this country from the border at the south to Hudson bay; I know it from Saint John to Vancouver. I have not said of Ontario that it is the greatest province in the world. I prefer to say that this could be the greatest country in the world. I prefer to say that our workers are getting top wages with United States labour. I prefer to say that a man can buy an automobile within reason in this country without being gouged $400 in taxes on his Ford car. I am speaking because I hope soon, owing to a greater population, taxes will be reduced due to the fact that we have a greater home market than we have today.
I would say: Go across the sparsely settled western provinces. I remember going across them with my father over fifty years ago, when he said to me: Son, when you are my age this country will have 50 million people. I have passed his age and he has passed to the great beyond, and we have 14 million people owing to nothing but lack of foresight on the part of the governments, both Conservative and Liberal, that we have had in power. We need in Canada today men like those who built the C.P.R. right across this country, who had vision and confidence, and who were willing to develop the gifts that God gave to Canadians in the way of great resources. This is not a gold mine in the St. Lawrence river. It is not an oil well. I believe all industries across this country should have been encouraged to develop themselves so they would all go along in harmony and this country would have developed into what it should be. I say that Canada's population today of 14 million people is an absolute disgrace to the planners of the past, particularly to the planners of the past 35 years. We have said that we do not want immigration here lest we be contaminated. My family have lived in this country for over 150 years; and when I cannot compete against a newcomer who cannot

even speak my language, the sooner I walk into the river until my hat floats, the better.
I have heard men who had good positions say: We do not want a melting pot here as in the United States. I heard one man say it today. I have heard another man in my own constituency say: We do not want these foreigners; they will take our jobs. I just looked at him in utter disgust. Just imagine a man who has been educated at the expense of the taxpayers of this country and who speaks the language prevalent in this country being afraid that a man who cannot even speak his language and who has half his education is going to take his job away. I have had men say: Well, these newcomers do not eat as well as we do. Let me say this. They ought to visit some of my foreign friends, where they do not get their food out of tin cans. They get it from the back garden, and it is succulent food at that. It is probably far more healthy than the stuff most of our Canadians are trying to eat. Just one excuse after another is offered. It is selfishness that holds back the growth of this country. It is time we members of this House of Commons spoke our minds and stopped this nonsense of Canada being talked of as a melting pot. Let us go ahead and encourage immigration. Let us bring artisans out here as well as farmers. Let us show them what we want them to do. Let us give them an opportunity of doing it.
Not many months ago a doctor from Rou-rnania arrived at our shores. His wife is a Viennese. There is one gentleman in the House of Commons who does not know what I am talking about. I have always advocated a loudspeaker system in this house so hon. gentlemen could hear the speeches. I am sure if that hon. member could hear what I am saying he would profit by it.
This doctor from Roumania to whom I referred, for the privilege of coming to Canada, the land of the free, had to wash dishes in a Gravenhurst sanatorium for one year. How can we expect our newcomers to tell their children what a great country we live in when they reflect back upon the sentence they had to serve on coming to the land of the free, namely washing dishes in a Gravenhurst sanatorium for one year. We are asking doctors to do that. That is the way we have been handling immigration. We should have a planned immigration scheme in this country. Bricklayers, carpenters and others should be coming here and being spread amongst all of the provinces of Canada to develop our country. Instead of doing that we are concentrating our thoughts on the St. Lawrence seaway. In my opinion the cart is being placed before the horse. I am not saying that it will not

be beneficial in years to come; but there are many items that are far more essential and on which the taxpayers' money could be spent at this time than the St. Lawrence waterway project.

speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
I wish to
make a few comments on this, Mr. Chairman. They are really inspired by the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings. I am going to vote for this resolution. I shall do it with certain questionings as to detail. It seems to me the leader of the opposition was right when he said that in a sense this is not a new plan, not a new design, not a new undertaking; it is merely to complete an existing undertaking. As I say, I propose to vote for it; but in saying that I should like to say also that I share some of the questions which have been raised as to whether this is going to be just as rosy all the way through as some people imagine. I could not help feeling this afternoon that the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings might have been warranted in raising certain questions as to whether this would immediately benefit the railways; whether it may be creating problems that none of us want to create. But I shall not take up the time of the committee on that. What I really want to do, speaking as an Ontario man, is say that I feel at the present time we are leaving our brethren from the maritimes in a position in which they should not be left.
We have listened to them this afternoon. We have heard the arguments they have made, and I do not think that we can regard them as trivial or unwarranted. Really all we have to say to them is: Come along. This is a big conception, a big project; it is going to be for the welfare of Canada, and you will be on the band wagon. You come along, and you will benefit like the rest of us. Well, the people in the maritimes have been hearing that for a long, long time, and I am not surprised that it sounds a little hollow. And although none of us intended it should be false, it may sound a little false to them. I do not mean that in the sense of being dishonest; I mean it is something which we may really intend, but which may never come true. I mean by that, it may never come true in any future near enough for them to be able to take much interest in it. There is no use talking to people who are going to live their lives in the next ten, twenty or thirty years and telling them that this will be a grand thing
St. Lawrence Waterway for their children or their grandchildren, and that they will benefit from it, because it is altogether likely that their children will have left the maritime provinces by that time.
It is not as if it were merely that they did not think this project would benefit them. They actually think it will do them harm, very substantial harm; and as one listens to them again, as I said a moment ago, it is awfully difficult to meet those arguments. The minister shakes his head. Perhaps he can meet them better than I can; but at any rate I am expressing my view for what it is worth. I find it very difficult to meet them. I will say this to the minister: No matter how persuasive he may be, I doubt very much whether even he will find arguments which are going to satisfy the people from the maritimes if things are left as they are at the moment. When I say "left as they are at the moment" what I mean is this. I submit the minister has done what has been done so often in the past. He is only holding out hopes to them that they will benefit. There is an exception to that. He pointed out that work would be provided in the maritimes by the iron ore production, but apart from that there was little enough hope. Indeed, as has been pointed out in the speeches which have been made, there was a great deal in his speech to alarm them and make them feel that actually not only would the seaway not help them but it would hurt them.
I want to go on from there to make this point. This afternoon the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings went a long way. I think he showed himself a true Canadian in his desire to find a common ground. He said in effect: "We want a common ground; we want to look at this in a broad sort of way. But there must be an over-all plan, not merely a plan which is going to come true in some vague far-off time which nobody can be sure of." In the past, of course, similar situations have existed; and I think in the past governments have been in difficulty because they did not have the means, unless they were going to abandon all their idea of government, to directly influence enterprises to establish here or there. They could do it to a small extent by taxation, but not to any very substantial extent.
My purpose in rising tonight, Mr. Chairman, is to point out that situation exists no longer; that the government now, if it wishes, has in its own hands the power to make definite statements as to what can be done, not this year, next year, sometime or never, but at once. My reason for saying that is what was explained to us this morning in the committee which is dealing with
1664	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway defence expenditures. 1666	HOUSE OF

speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
What that means I do not know, and I am sure members of this house do not know. That is why I prefaced my remarks with the statement that I thought this to be a rather strange debate. Most hon. members got up and said this was a good thing provided it was beneficial to all parts of Canada, and then many hon. members proceeded, either in their own words or with documented evidence, to give arguments against it. I would like to deal with the arguments that were given against it, and I do this in answer to what the hon. member for Greenwood said. I do not pretend that I shall be able to answer all his arguments or that I shall be able to satisfy members from the maritimes, but I shall attempt to answer the arguments as I understand them and I will do it with all the sincerity of purpose of which I am capable.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South began his remarks the other night by stating that the united mineworkers of his constituency were against it, and he put on the record seven reasons why they were against it. He then proceeded to say that they had made a series of careful researches over a period of time and found that they were against it. Why were they against it? Because it was going to be a danger to their livelihood. What I intend to say in reply to that is not said with the slightest idea of disparaging the united mineworkers. I am sure it will not be taken as such, either by them or by my friend.
Over the last fifty years Canada has been studying this project and has had at least ten or twelve reports strongly in favour of it. It began away back in 1919 when the international joint commission, after having given it the most careful study, decided that power and navigation should be developed on the St. Lawrence. Later on they appointed a joint board of United States and Canadian engineers which went into the matter most carefully and decided it was a good thing for Canada. Then later on both countries appointed a board composed of three Canadian engineers and three United States engineers who studied it for several years and came to the conclusion that it was a good thing for Canada from the point of view of engineering and economy as well. The 

international joint commission gave it further consideration and again reported in favour of it.
Then there was convened in Ottawa in 1928 a conference of Canadian engineers who gave it their unqualified approval. Later on-this will reply in part to some of the allegations made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South concerning the lukewarmness of the province of Quebec-a board composed of one Quebec engineer, one Ontario engineer and one federal engineer declared themselves in favour of this project.
In 1932 a treaty was signed by Canada and the United States known as the treaty of Washington. This supported the project, the only difference being that it was to be a two-stage development instead of one-stage, with a control dam. The Prime Minister of that time was a maritimer. Surely he must have weighed the arguments for and against the part of the country from which he had originally come. He declared himself in favour of the scheme. Then in 1941 a government headed by the late W. L. Mackenzie King signed the great lakes and St. Lawrence basin agreement. That was done only after careful consideration. Economic studies were made by various departments of government, a recent one being by the Department of Trade and Commerce which was made in 1951. After careful investigation they concluded that this was a good thing, not for one part but for all parts of Canada.
The last but not the least of the arguments which I think should be replied to and which was put forward not so much by the hon. member for Cape Breton South as by the hon. member for Royal, and the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings, was that by no stretch of the imagination could this be conceived as a defence project. They asked by what means this could be considered as being helpful to defence. My answer is that the permanent joint board on defence composed of United States and Canadian representatives gave this project most careful consideration. Let me read the evidence given by none other than Hon. Dean Acheson, Secretary of State of the United States of America, before the committee on public works of the United States congress. He said:
Our reliance on Canada, and Canada's reliance on us, is not confined to the economic or political field. From a military point of view the defence of the United States cannot be conducted independently of the defence of Canada. The two countries compose a single defensive unit. This fact was officially recognized in 1940 when the permanent joint board on defence was established to consider means by which the United States and Canada could co-operate more fully for their common security. This board functions today with increasing effectiveness and earlier this month it, made a

joint recommendation concerning the military value of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project. The board's statement is as follows:
"The board re-examined the St. Lawrence seaway and power project in the light of the serious international situation and the needs of the continental defence. The board also reaffirmed the value of the project in peacetime and considered anew its immediate importance in terms of the present-day defence of the northern half of this continent.
"Since the board's previous recommendations of May, 1947, and December, 1948, the international situation had deteriorated markedly. In the Far East, there had already been fighting which involved both Canada and the United States. Other dangerous situations which might lead to open combat involving our two nations existed in other parts of the world. It appeared that the free nations might be entering a period of protracted crisis during which it was imperative that our military strength be steadily increased.
"In view of these ominous circumstances, the board believed it had a duty again to recommend early construction of the St. Lawrence seaway and power project. The project would yield additional supplies of hydroelectric power-supplies which were already needed in the northeastern United States and eastern Canada, and which later would become vital to the expansion of our military strength. The seaway would provide an inland waterway relatively safe from enemy action. It would enable the two countries to move war materials at less cost in money and resources than by any other means. In addition, the seaway would permit greatly increased shipbuilding and ship repairs in the relatively well protected great lakes shipyards.
I am not making that statement.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Would the minister explain why the United States turned it down after such a strong recommendation?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
In a moment, I am going to deal with the very argument you brought up, but I should like to say now that these are not my words. These are the words of the Secretary of State of the United States, who also quotes the permanent joint board on defence. He continues with the statement of the permanent joint board on defence as follows:
The diminution of the iron ore supplies of the Mesabi range, coupled with the discovery and development of large new deposits of high grade ore in Labrador, constituted an added reason for immediate commencement of work on the project. Since Labrador iron ore could be transported most economically by ship to the large steel producing centres of the great lakes, the value of the Labrador mines, so necessary to defence industry, could be fully exploited only by building the seaway. In the board's opinion the addition which the project would make to our military potential would far outweigh the initial expenditure in manpower, money and critical materials. Much of these materials would be required in any event because if the combined project for navigation and power were not now proceeded with alternative sources of power would have to be provided. The board recognized the risk to the St. Lawrence seaway project from enemy attack. It was of the opinion, however, that this risk was no greater than the danger to many other existing installations of comparable importance. Since the area concerned was already one of high defence priority, the board believed that adequate protective measures would 94699-107
St. Lawrence Waterway be possible on a reasonably economic basis. Having in mind these considerations and reaffirming its previous recommendation, the board recommended: "That the two governments take immediate action to implement the 1941 St. Lawrence agreement as a vital measure for their common defence."
I have cited that at [DOT] some length for the simple reason that I felt the words I had uttered in my original statement did not suffice. Therefore I bring to my support not only the statement of Dean Acheson but also the statement of the permanent joint board on defence. Then I go on to the second argument raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He said-and I presume I am not misquoting him when I say he referred to the supporting documents which he had from the united mine workers union- that if this project goes through they fear that the coal industry in the maritime provinces will be made to disappear. My answer to that is twofold. First I say that we have just concluded a debate on railway legislation. I say that we have also had the benefit of the report of the royal commission on transportation. I say that the maritime provinces were represented by very able counsel before that royal commission, who brought forward the point of view of the maritimes. What did they say to the royal commission? In effect they said: We live in a far-away part of the country in so far as the central markets are concerned. Therefore we have a long haul to get into those markets and very often we have an equally long haul to bring back our raw materials to the maritime provinces. We have not, like the central provinces, highway competition and the like. Our economy, they said, is one which should normally move from north to south but because of confederation it has been forced to move from east to west. I do not think anyone will challenge my statement, because I think those are the facts. The maritime provinces complained at that time, and with reason and justice, that that position created a disadvantage in so far as they were concerned.
Having said to the royal commission on transportation that that was the position in which they found themselves, namely that there was this long rail haul to the markets and the long haul back, surely when an open seaway is offered, when an alternative route is offered whereby they can move their products not only into the Montreal market but into the great Toronto market and the markets of the great lakes, to my way of thinking that has relieved the situation to some extent. Then I add that not only is the position relieved by the construction of the seaway; it is also relieved by the fact

St. Lawrence Waterway that rates will be equalized in the rest of Canada. East-west rates will be reduced because of the subsidy of $7 million which will be paid and because of the one and one-third rule. The maritimes will also get the benefit of that. I submit, with deference, that is an answer to the point raised by my hon. friend when he says that their livelihood will be made to disappear on account of the construction of the seaway.

speechtext: The minister has just confirmed what I said.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
The next argument I make has to do with the coal industry. What is the position of that industry? Without wanting to disagree with my hon. friend, or with the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings and the hon. member for Royal in their summation of the position in so far as the coal industry is concerned, I do not think they need be so apprehensive as they were in their speeches because I do not think the position they put on Hansard is an accurate one. I have before me statistics furnished by the bureau of statistics which indicate the distribution of Nova Scotia coal production. With the consent of the house I should like to place it on Hansard. It indicates that the total Nova Scotia production of coal in 1939 was 6,857,000 tons, and the total production of Nova Scotia coal in 1950 was 6,517,000 tons. The point I wish to make is that of the total of 6,857,000 tons in 1939, some
3.743.000	tons were used in the maritimes and 3,114,000 tons were shipped to central Canada, Quebec and Ontario, whereas in 1950 of the 6,517,000 tons of coal produced in Nova Scotia 4,717,000 were used for local consumption and only 1,800,000 were moved into Quebec and Ontario.
The point I am making is that the table indicates that the demand for coal within the maritime provinces has increased from
3.743.000	tons in 1939 to 4,717,000 tons in 1950. In other words, local demand consumed 55 per cent of the production in 1939 and 72 per cent in 1950. These are facts. At this rate the full production will be consumed in the maritimes in another ten or fifteen years. The simple fact, as I understand the problem, appears to be that Nova Scotia coal already is withdrawing from the central Canada markets. Before the war as much as 2,300,000 tons of maritime coal were shipped into Quebec in one year and as much as 1,300,000 tons into Ontario. The total shipment of Nova Scotia coal to central Canada in 1939 was 3,114,000 tons. The decline is not for want of transportation facilities or assistance, and certainly not for lack of demand; because if I correctly recall the statement made by

the president of the Canadian National Railways in the committee on railways and shipping it was that the Canadian National Railways could have taken another 1,100,000 tons of Nova Scotia coal if it had been available. It was not available, and the railway had to obtain coal from the United States. I believe it can safely be said that at least another 2 million tons of coal would have been required in the central market. What is happening to Nova Scotia coal is simply this. Because of requirements for power production, coal for their own employees, for their own collieries, for bunkers, for railways in the maritimes, for their steel plants and for Newfoundland, the maritimes are gradually using up the full production of coal. If I have permission I should like to put this table on Hansard.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

I am not admitting, therefore, the premise of my hon. friend's argument. The point I am trying to make-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: The point I am making now is that according to the table I have put on Hansard the maritime people are gradually consuming greater amounts of their own coal production. maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to point out that Nova Scotia has an objective of 10 million tons per year; that has been the objective for a long time. We must allow our production to diminish, and we are not to expect the expansion of that industry in order to market coal in central Canada.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Nothing that is going to be done under this resolution or either of the two bills following will affect the production of coal, as I see it.
If I may I should like to go on with the other point made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), and I believe supported by other hon. members, although my memory does not serve me sufficiently well to be able to quote them, and perhaps they may get up and say I am mistaken in the statement. In any event the point was
St. Lawrence Waterway made by the member for Cape Breton South: why export iron ore? I believe the words he used were these: To whom are we making the iron ore available? Why export iron ore? Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I need answer that argument, because the people of this country answered it many years ago. What happened to our gold and our silver in northern Ontario and northern Quebec? Did we not decide to export it? Were not whole groups of communities established in both provinces because of that development, and because of that policy to export those natural resources? What happened to the lake St. John district in the province of Quebec in which aluminum is being produced? A whole area that was undeveloped and uncolonized for many years was developed because the aluminum industry came there and exported the product to the United Kingdom, the United States and perhaps to other countries. A series of communities was built along that area.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Do they export the raw ore or do they refine it?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Will my hon friend allow me to continue? My hon. friend made his speech. He is at liberty to make another speech if he wishes.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the minister.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to reply to the arguments that are being made, but if I am to be interrupted continually it is rather difficult to make an argument.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I believe it is proper that we should deal with these points as we go along. I should like to ask the minister whether his argument applies to the great pulpwood industry. Is he opposed to having the pulpwood manufactured into its final form here, or should we go back 25 years or more and ship it in the rawest form possible to the United States.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will only hold his peace I shall deal with pulpwood in a moment. At the moment I am dealing with this argument: why should we export iron ore? I ask your permission, Mr. Chairman, to be allowed to continue. If there are any questions I will do the best I can to answer them afterwards. When I am attempting to answer this argument I do not think it is fair that I should be subjected to continual interruptions from the other side. I said, why did we decide to export Steep Rock ore? Why was it that we decided to export copper and nickel from northern Manitoba? Why did this house at the last session vote substantial

St. Lawrence Waterway sums of money to the Canadian National Railways to help develop the nickel and copper deposits at Lynn Lake by the building of a railway? What about oil in Alberta? Is it a crime to export aluminum from Kitimat? At the next session of parliament I hope to be in a position to introduce a bill which will, I trust, bring about the construction of a railway from Kitimat to join with the Prince Rupert-Prince George line. In this area there will be a tremendous aluminum development, and I am informed a white man has never put his foot on that spot. Why do we do that?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: To keep on exporting the aluminum we have instead of manufacturing it; that is why we do it.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: If the hon. member wants to follow his argument to its logical conclusion, why do we export wheat?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: We do not export any more than the surplus we have. My argument is that we are not manufacturing enough in this country; we are exporting.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: All right. That is exactly what we are going to do, as I see it. That is exactly what we are doing with aluminum. That is exactly what we are doing with all these natural resources.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: This country exports-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: We do not export any more than we have surplus to our own requirements; and if that is the case, I think that is a reply to the argument raised by my hon. friends. I could go on and say this. If our friends on the other side of the line were to adopt the same argument, where would we in central Canada get our coal? Where would we get our oil, our cotton, our steel, our rubber or our tin?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: You can get anything you want.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Those are questions that I think are significant answers to those raised by the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
Another point that was made was this: Why not build up our mills in our own country? On that point, Mr. Chairman, I find myself in agreement with the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings and the leader of the opposition, who did not go nearly as far as did the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings or the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: He did not understand as well.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
He said: I have no objection to exporting ore provided we see to it that

some assistance is given to our own mills.
I hope it will be possible to do that, and that takes me to the point raised by the hon. member for Cumberland with respect to pulpwood and the paper industry. That was a point made by the leader of the opposition, namely that in the pulpwood industry and in the timber industry we were able to place certain conditions on the export of this pulpwood, when we stipulated that mills for the production and fabrication of paper would be established in our own country, as they have been.
But the position as to pulpwood compared with the position as to iron ore is as day is to night. In pulpwood and in timber we have a monopoly; but in iron ore we are not in that fortunate position. In iron ore we are in a competitive position. We have to compete with iron ore from Liberia, from Venezuela and from other countries. We therefore cannot stipulate. Then again, when I say "we cannot" I refer unquestionably to the provincial governments; and I say this without the slightest desire to be disparaging of them, because these are matters which concern provincial governments. The timber rights and the rights concerning iron ore in Ungava and Newfoundland are those arising out of provincial jurisdiction; and if anyone can tie down the owners, it is the provincial governments. But I am saying that the position, so far as a provincial government is concerned, with reference to iron ore is entirely different from that with reference to pulp and paper.
Then again it has been suggested that Canadians do not want to be merely hewers of wood and drawers of water. I agree with those sentiments. I wish to make it clear that I am not disparaging in any sense the hewers of wood and the drawers of water; but that is not the point. The point is that we want other Canadians to work on the wood and on the water too, in shaping them to their ultimate uses. In this case, that of iron ore, we want Canadians to have the opportunity of mining it and moving it to market. We hope also that other Canadians will have a large share-the larger the better -in the smelting of the iron, in producing the steel, yes and in fabricating the steel into finished products. The production of steel ingots and castings in Canada, for instance, has increased from a total of 1,551,000 net tons in 1939 to a total of 3,383,000 in 1950. I am not able to say what the production is in Nova Scotia, because this concerns one company alone and I am not at liberty to produce the figures I have; but I may say

that the Nova Scotia production was substantial and that province has shared tremendously in the expansion which I have just mentioned.
There is no evidence-certainly none on the record so far in this debate-that the completion of the seaway will put an end to the expansion of Nova Scotia's steel industry. As a matter of fact it appears that some reduction in the cost of production, possibly a substantial one, can be effected by mixing Labrador ore with Wabana ore in the blast furnaces. Iron and steel costs may be further reduced to the extent that the cost of coal is lowered by the mechanization now under way in the coal mines. All these forces will, I think, tend to strengthen the steel industry not only in other parts of Canada but in the maritime provinces as well. The day before yesterday I had the good fortune of discussing this very problem with one greatly concerned with the production of steel in the maritime province of Nova Scotia. He immediately said to me: The seaway will not in the slightest degree harm our steel industry in Nova Scotia.
I now go on to the point which was made concerning navigation being window dressing for power. It has been suggested that we are not serious about the navigation, that it is only a question of window dressing. The federal government is using its best efforts, in this resolution and in the bills which will follow, to assist Ontario in developing
1.100.000	horsepower in the international rapids section of the river where it is required by that province. Then, in case my hon. friend should think that the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs sometime ago was indicative that there was a snag in Quebec, let me assure him that there is no snag in the province of Quebec; because there at Lachine it is hoped it will be possible to develop a joint power and navigation scheme as a result of which
1.200.000	horsepower of electrical energy will be produced. What prompts me to make the statement is that some two years ago I tabled in the House of Commons a joint report made by a board established by this government

the chairman was Mr. R. A. C. Henry, a prominent engineer of Montreal, a former deputy minister of the Department of Transport, a former chairman of the air transport board and a former officer of the Canadian National Railways-together with the Quebec hydro, in which several plans were submitted for the production of power and the development of navigation at Lachine. One of them particularly was recommended. It had to do with a joint power and navigation scheme at Lachine.
St. Lawrence Waterway
My hon. friend spoke disparagingly, I thought-I am sure he did not mean to do so but it looked to me as though he did-of the statement made in western Canada by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce. He spoke disparagingly, I thought, of his statement which he quoted to this effect: The St. Lawrence seaway must be built. Without it the steel industry now on the great lakes would have to migrate to the Atlantic coast.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: That statement was made in the United States.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I am not denying that it was made there.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: You said the statement was made in the west.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
I accept the correction. But the point I am making now is that surely that statement, taken out of its context, means an entirely different thing than if read with the context. What the Minister of Trade and Commerce was referring to unquestionably was the migration of steel industries to the Atlantic sea coast of the United States. And the argument he was probably making-I have not his text before me-was that it would be much better for us to take our iron ore in Labrador and Quebec and move it up to the great lakes, through the St. Lawrence seaway, and there sell it where there is a market, than leave it where it is doing nothing. That is the position I think he took.
Then he referred to shipbuilding in the great lakes, as I did, too. I think my friend the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings misunderstood or misinterpreted, not intentionally I am sure, the statement I had made. I had no intention of saying anything concerning the shipyards on the Atlantic coast. I was dealing with one thing only, and that was the great lakes-St. Lawrence seaway for defence purposes. I was trying to make the point that if we had the seaway we could build there, in an area which would be practically invulnerable to attack, destroyers, submarines, escort vessels, trawlers and the like, which could be taken down the deep waterway for defence purposes. That is the point I was trying to make, and I think it is exactly the point the permanent joint board on defence made. Certainly there could be no damage done to our maritime yards on the St. Lawrence river or on the Atlantic coast, because at the moment 1 think they have a considerable number of orders.
The hon. member for Annapolis-Kings discussed the question of finance. He will excuse me if I do not go into that now, because I do not think this is the stage to
1672	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway do that. There are financial sections in the bill which we will come to at the appropriate time. But I think the main point he made, and which I have not referred to up to now, is the adverse effect that this will have on the railways. Well, I made what I thought was a fairly considerable explanation of the position of the railways. Apparently it did not satisfy my hon. friend, and I do not think it satisfied the hon. member for Royal. However, he is entitled to his opinion. Perhaps if he will not take my argument he will at least take the argument of the president of the Canadian National Railways when he spoke to the railways and shipping committee-

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
I would rather take the
minister's.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
-on March 25, 1949. Mr. Hazen asked this question:
There Is another matter you referred to in addition to truck and air competition: you referred to the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways. Now, you must have made some study on that, I presume?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Yes, sir.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: What losses in revenue, or in railway business, do you anticipate if the St. Lawrence waterway is deepened?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: We had our research and development department, and bureau of economies make a thorough study of that situation, because we were very anxious to know what traffic we might lose if the canals were deepened. After giving the matter much study and making a thorough investigation their report is, as I recall it, that they do not expect the railway will suffer any substantial loss of business at all because they consider that there will be so many new industries built up along these new waterways that the business we would get from these new industries would more than make up for what we might lose in any other direction. Mr. Hazen: When was that report made?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
That report was made two or
three years ago.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Was it in 1947, or 1948, or prior to
that time?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
In any event that was the conclusion. Mr. Vaughan:	I remember distinctly that the
conclusion reached in the report forecast no great loss of business. The report was made about two years ago but I cannot give you the exact date.
The successor to Mr. Vaughan, Mr. Donald Gordon, is of the same view and has so declared on more than one occasion in public statements. I think I am not taking too much upon myself when I say it is our view that the Canadian Pacific Railway are of the same opinion.
I have spoken altogether too long, Mr. Chairman. I had no intention of being so lengthy, but I did want to assure the committee and the hon. member for Cape Breton South that, like himself, I too am a Canadian and I believe in the development of our Canadian resources. If I did not I probably would not be in the house at all, because those who sent me here felt that was one of the first duties that I owed to them and to


this parliament. That, too, is the duty of the government. It feels that the resources of the country should be developed. Unquestionably, both from the point of view of power and the point of view of navigation, as well as from the point of view of iron ore and all the allied industries that will come out of it, those resources will mean a great deal to the economy of Canada. And to those who say that the taxpayers cannot foot the bill I say: wait a little while and see what the bill contains. I think it will be established, I hope beyond doubt, that it will be possible, as I stated in my initial speech, to self-liquidate the whole navigation part of -this scheme by means of -the imposition of tolls. With that, Mr. Chairman, I hope it will be possible to get on with the resolution.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: Why is that?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
They can make more money, and it is cheaper to import the coal and get the drawback from the government. That point the minister brought out in his figures. We are not putting any coal at all into Ontario at this time. Another thing of which I would remind the minister in connection with the production figures he gave us is that at least three large coal-producing collieries, namely collieries Nos. 2 and 11, and the Allen shaft, have closed, but which were operating on that short-week basis. One of them employed 1,500 men, but they have closed down since.
So the production figures do not help the minister's case at all. They merely prove what I have been saying over the years, that so far as that industry is concerned there is no national vision. It is a matter of shrinking the industry to cater to the market handiest to them, while they import coal from the United States and fill the market for which they themselves should be reaching.
St. Lawrence Waterway

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: I should like to make one comment. The hon. member is making a most admirable case. Everyone is rejoicing because of the work he is doing; a man who comes from the mines, and who can express himself so admirably here in the House of Commons. I compliment him in the highest measure. I should like to ask him one or two questions so that he may enlighten us with his answers. Can he give us any connection between this shrinkage and any economic factor the impact of which is likely to be intensified by the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: That is a poser.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
No, that is not a poser. There is no particular economic factor in Nova Scotia that would work to the detriment of that industry, due to the building of the St. Lawrence seaway. But there is one point, and I was just about to discuss it. The minister made the statement again that the opening of the seaway would increase the opportunity of putting Nova Scotia coal on the Ontario market, and that it would not affect the future of that industry at all. He pointed out the argument related to subsidies, subventions and the like, as applied to long hauls. Let me point out to him that we already have our water route. We can ship from Louisburg and Sydney-more particularly from Louisburg, which is open all winter-by way of the St. Lawrence during the months it is open. Indeed that method of shipment could be used nearly all winter, if necessary, although the insurance is lifted at the end of eight months.
I am pointing out that we already have that water route for the shipment of Canadian coal. The only reason we are able to stay in the Montreal market is that it is the only market that is economical so far as Nova Scotia coal is concerned. We stay in that market because the Americans cannot get in there by a water route. Even now the coal marketed in Quebec is subsidized by the federal government to enable it to get in there on a competitive basis with United States coal, even with the handicap of the rail haul. Therefore, instead of doing what the minister suggests it will do, namely expand the market for us, it will open up a water route and cheapen transportation for United States coal. This will back the Nova Scotia product out of the Montreal market.
I am not blaming the government for the policy of shrinking the industry, and for the fact that the Dominion Steel and Coal Company has gone into the importing
1674	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway business. That is entirely a matter of the policy of the company, and it is one I have kicked around for a long time.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: May I interrupt again by asking another question? I am looking for a solution, of course. If the dominion government were to agree to a subsidy on Nova Scotia coal, to offset the advantage given to the United States, would that not obviate the difficulty mentioned by the hon. member?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
No; I think it is false economy to spend $400 million to build a seaway which will give the Americans the advantage in that market, and then ask the taxpayers of Canada to subsidize the movement of one of our own resources into a market they have already paid to get. There is a limit to the extent to which we can keep going down into the pockets of the taxpayers.
Let me point out to the minister that his arguments with respect to the coal situation are not valid. I am not criticizing him. I would not argue stare decisis with him; that is his field. But in this particular field let ' me tell him that I have a lot of kinks in my spine from shovelling coal, which was my business for years. I am not biased; I like to be fair; but when a company follows a faulty policy in developing an industry, and follows the line of least resistance by shrinking the industry, and leans on the arm of the government wherever it can, as well as going into the importing business because it is cheaper and perhaps more lucrative, I believe I am called upon to say something. It is not building a Canadian industry.
One other point I would like to make, in respect of what the minister had to say. On the point as to why we should export our iron ore, my answer is that we should export our surplus. I have no objection to that. But we should not be in the position of simply developing and opening up our raw materials in order to make them available to the United States. As far as steel is concerned, we are completely dependent today upon the United States. The scream all the time is that we cannot get steel for automobiles and for our defence requirements. I know of one city that wants to get a 200,000 gallon boiler for the water supply in one important section and they cannot get it because there is no steel. If we are not able to supply our own requirements in steel the logical thing for us to do is to export our surplus ore. That is what we are doing with wheat. I think it is wrong to think just in terms of opening up our raw materials and making them available to the United States.
I say to the minister that this business of depending on the United States is going to
fMr. Gillis.]

catch up with us some day unless we are going to sit by and be absorbed by them. We must make up our minds one way or another. The minister said that we are dependent upon the United States for coal. That is quite true, but we should not be. The minister asks where we would get coal. We can get it in New Brunswick, in Nova Scotia, in Saskatchewan, in Alberta in unlimited supply and in British Columbia. It is merely a matter of developing our own resources and freeing ourselves from the economic dictatorship which the United States can wield if they so desire. The same thing is true of steel. This country should not be in the position of having to import steel to meet our ordinary requirements. As I suggested when I spoke before, I am prepared to support this project as one part of a large public investment program by the federal government. This authority to be set up should have the right to develop any potential power or other resource within a reasonable distance of that area.
I should like to point out to the minister that steel production in this country is not as great as it should be. It is no good going back to 1939 because we were in a pretty bad way from the production standpoint in that year. When you start with 1948 you really get at the place where we began to slip with a lot of things. I put the figures on record a couple of days ago when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was present. In the last fifteen months the production of basic steel in this country has been stationary while production in the United States has gone up from 35 to 40 per cent. They are really going ahead down there.
I think the government would be well advised to have another basic steel plant. This would not be asking very much. We would still be exporting our raw materials to the large centres for fabrication. The steel plant at Sydney employs about 4,500 men in the manufacture of basic steel. I do not care where you pick a site, in Pictou county or in Prince Edward Island or in Newfoundland; you would still be close to the raw materials. A new plant could be set up or the Sydney plant could be expanded, possibly by the use of public funds. That would cure a lot of problems. A market would be provided for what Prince Edward Island is producing. I should like to see enough industry down in that part of the country to absorb all the production of the maritimes. It is not asking very much to say that we should try to stand on our own feet in this matter of using raw materials. Another instance is the aluminum industry.

There is no excuse for allowing United States capital to come in here and develop the great aluminum industry practically at the expense of the taxpayers of Canada. The headquarters of that industry is in the United States, and the control lies in that country. The same thing is true in connection with pulpwood. Go down along the New Brunswick border and take a look at what is happening. People from the United States have been coming there to lease our timber lands and cut our pulpwood. They have a belt line running across the border to take the raw materials over there to be processed into paper which we buy back at $90 per ton.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: More than that.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext: It was $90 the last time I heard about it, and that is bad enough. I am quite sticky on this business of looking after ourselves first. If we have any surplus we can export it as we do with wheat. I am not going to argue any longer. I have stated my case, and I simply wanted .to straighten out the minister on these production figures. Instead of hurting my case all he has done is confirm what I suspected right along, that there is no intention to look after maritime needs. I suggest to the minister that it is nearly .time that we developed our own resources, such as coal, for ourselves. With the potential supplies of coal we have we should not have to depend upon the United States to the extent we do at the present time. We should not have to face a recurrence of the fuel crisis on the Canadian National which we had a couple of years ago.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the minister seems to want to rush through this important legislation, about which a great many people in my part of the country have considerable doubt. Some of the members from down there have expressed trepidation as to what the results will be. I think we should have all these matters cleared up. I am not going to delay the committee but I just want to express my views. I have expressed them before and they are on record.
I am not opposed, as one good Canadian in a family which has done a lot over the years in making Canada possible, to the development of this country or to the development of the power resources in central Canada, but I want to know what there is for Nova Scotia and the maritime provinces to compensate for the contribution they have made to Canada and to give them the place they should have in confederation. We should
St. Lawrence Waterway have a more definite statement from the minister and the government at this time than the minister gave today or a few days ago. I am not opposed to what is being done in central Canada, but I am not satisfied with what is being done to develop our resources in Nova Scotia. I am opposed to having this go through until there is further discussion.
Progress reported.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF CERTAIN PETITIONS TO COMMITTEE ON STANDING ORDERS

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime
Minister): I understand that the clerk of petitions has laid on the table four petitions from religious bodies for private bills. It had not been intended, as hon. members know, to have any private bills dealt with at this session; but it has been represented to us, and to the leaders of the other groups of the house, that with respect to these four bills they were intended to relieve their anxieties about some possible illegality in the investment of trust funds of these religious bodies; and after discussing the matter with the leaders of other groups I felt we might ask for unanimous consent to make an exception for these religious bodies, it being still understood this will be the only exception, and that none will be made for any private interests.
The petitions are from the general synod of the Church of England in Canada and the missionary society of the Church of England in Canada, for an act authorizing them to consolidate, manage and invest the trust funds under their control as one fund to be known as the Church of England consolidated trust fund, and for other incidental purposes. I understand that these trust funds are now in a provincially incorporated trust
company, and that as the investments are made in more than one province in Canada the synod of the Anglican church has been advised that there may be some illegality in their proceedings, and they are quite anxious to have that removed at the earliest possible opportunity.
The other is from the Sisters of Charity of the House of Providence of Kingston, Ontario, for an act to incorporate the Sisters of Providence. They have provincial charters in several of the provinces, but they also have the same body of assets distributed throughout several provinces, and they have been advised that their position in that regard is not strictly in conformity with our general laws.
The next one is from Edward G. Wheeler and others, of Langham, Saskatchewan, representing Canadians of the Mennonite brotherhood. They are applying for the usual incorporation as a recognized church society. It was felt that if any exception were made for any one of these groups the exception would have to extend to the other two, because it would be felt, I was sure, by all members of the house, that there should be no discrimination between them on religious grounds. But again I wish to assure the house that it is not intended to make any exception for any private interests. It is only because these are semi-public bodies that it was felt the house might be prepared to allow a special exception in their regard. I move, therefore:
That the following petitions for private bills presented on December 6. 1951, together with the report made thereon by the clerk of petitions on December 7, 1951, be referred to the standing committee on standing orders for such recommendations as may be deemed advisable in relation to standing orders 92 and 93(3) (a) and (b), namely:
Of the general synod of the Church of England in Canada, and the missionaary society of the Church of England in Canada, for an act authorizing them to consolidate, manage and invest the trust funds under their control as one fund to be known as the Church of England consolidated trust fund, and for other purposes.
Of the general synod of the Church of England in Canada, for an act amending its act of incorporation with respect to investment of its funds, and for other purposes.
Of the Sisters of Charity of the House of Providence at Kingston, Ontario, for an act to incorporate the Sisters of Providence.
Of Edward G. Wheeler and others, of Langham, Saskatchewan, for an act to incorporate Evangelical Mennonite Brethren of Canada.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NATIONAL EMPLOYMENT SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. To what extent do the offices of the national employment service recognize the labour laws of the various provinces in which national employment service offices are located, when making referrals? If there are any exceptions, will the minister give an explanation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: NATIONAL EMPLOYMENT SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for York South warned me that he was going to ask this question. In reply I think I could not do better than quote the pertinent instructions issued to officers of the national employment service of the unemployment insurance' commission. Those instructions are:
When, orders are listed with any local office by an. employer, and when such orders do not offer the minimum wages or working conditions specifically required by dominion statute or regulation, or by provincial statute or regulation, any variation from prescribed conditions will be brought to the attention of the employer in order that he may have opportunity to make correction. Only if the employer fails to make such correction, should the office refuse to undertake to fill the vacancies listed. The fact that an applicant may be willing to accept employment at a standard lower than that prescribed by governmental regulations furnishes no warrant whatever for the office to make a placement at less than the standard.
It is the responsibility of each local office to keep itself informed of all statutes or regulations fixing wages and working conditions in its district. These may include the fair wage schedules set by the Department of Labour regulating rates of pay on,

dominion government contracts; minimum rates of pay for workers fixed by the minimum wage board of the province; wage rates called for in legalized wage agreements between groups of employers and employees; and any other comparable legislation or regulations which may be issued from time to time.
As to the last part of the question, in which the hon. member asked me to give an explanation, if there are any exceptions, I would say that, in reality, there are no exceptions. But if an employer quotes in his order to the national employment service less than the provincial minimum rate of wages, the matter is drawn to his attention and, if he corrects it, nothing further is done.
