maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Thursday, December 6, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Chevrier-Mr. Dion in the chair:
That it is expedient, for the purpose of providing a deep waterway between Montreal and lake Erie, to create a corporation to be called "the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority" with power, inter alia, to expropriate; to construct, maintain and operate all necessary works; to borrow amounts not exceeding three hundred million dollars; to establish tariffs of tolls and to employ such officers and employees as may be required for the purposes of the authority.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY AUTHORITY  DEEP WATERWAY BETWEEN MONTREAL AND LAKE ERIE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in previous sessions, and again yesterday, I have stated that I am not opposed to a deep waterway serving central Canada and for the development of power resources, but I am
St. Lawrence Waterway interested in any menace there may be to the interests of the maritime provinces. I am interested in what compensating expenditures are proposed to benefit my part of the country.
I am very much disappointed in the statement of the minister, in that there appears to be no compensating expenditure proposed which would be of direct benefit to the maritime provinces. Instead, to some extent our interests are menaced. In addition we have to make a very definite contribution to the provision of $300 million, and probably double that amount, for the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. From every standpoint I say there should be a statement from the minister as to what is proposed by way of direct assistance to us in Nova Scotia, and the other maritime provinces. There is the question of the Chignecto canal. The minister made a personal investigation of the St. Lawrence seaway and brought in direct recommendations involving large expenditures, but even though it comes under his department he has not made a similar investigation of the proposal to build the Chignecto canal which has been before Canada ever since confederation and even before that time. A large delegation made representations on behalf of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and I believe Newfoundland, for the building of the Chignecto canal, but they were brushed aside. Nothing is being done. This is an opportune time for the minister to state what is proposed with respect to the Chignecto canal and what compensating expenditures will be made to us for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway and power projects.
I made a statement on June 7, 1951, and at that time I asked the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) whether he had made an inspection of the Chignecto canal. At that time I said, and I quote from page 3840 of Hansard:
I doubt whether the minister has made an inspection of the Chignecto canal and whether he gave support to its construction when a very large delegation came here. It was rather enlightening to see the interest which the Minister of Transport took in the proposed St. Lawrence seaway. He accompanied a large delegation over the St. Lawrence river inspecting that part of the river in which the seaway is proposed to be built at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars, and perhaps a billion dollars, which would give cheap power to central Canada when constructed. I do not say that I am opposed to that expenditure, but I would expect some compensating expenditures in my part of the country.
I again put that question to the minister and to the government. I repeat that this is an opportune time to have a statement. We are a part of Canada and we have rights in Canada. We have the right to expect the
1680	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway adoption of policies that will be of direct benefit to us. Originally we had vested rights in the hinterland of Quebec and the great iron ore deposits in Quebec belonged to Nova Scotia as one of the original provinces. We are receiving no benefit from the development of that great resource. The same applies to the great nickel industry in central Canada; no direct benefit accrues'to us in that connection. I think we have certain rights in the power development on the St. Lawrence. We were interested in the seaway at the time of confederation and I think we have some rights there. The same would apply to the great oil deposits in Alberta and western Canada. We are not receiving any benefit in that connection and in many others that I could cite.
In 1947 I quoted figures to show that up to that time there had been expended in Canada for canals a total of $243,352,399.78; practically all in central Canada, and hardly a dollar in our part of the country. There had been paid out for deficits and maintenance on the canals a total of $114,130,209.81 up to that time, with hardly a dollar of that being expended in the maritime provinces.
Then there is the question of shipbuilding. Shipbuilding is the birthright of the maritime provinces. At the time of confederation we had scores of shipyards and I contend that that industry should be developed and not be permitted to follow the lead given by the Minister of Transport when he proposed, I suppose in encouragement of central Canada, that there should be a further development of shipyards in central Canada but nothing for us in the east. That was confirmed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) who stated a short time ago that shipyards are to be developed in central Canada. No hope is held out by the minister or the government of a development in our part of Canada.
I say that we are entitled to that. That is our birthright as Nova Scotians who came into confederation eighty odd years ago. There is nothing in this proposal now before us which holds out any hope of any development in our part of the country. Most shipyards are developed by direct appropriations by the government for naval or transport purposes. The government not only has the power, it has the duty to allocate expenditures to our part of Canada, especially as we have not fared as we should have fared under confederation. We have always been prepared to make our contribution, but there is never any development for us. The government is spending $300 to $600 million here and more than that for power development, but there is nothing whatever for our part of Canada.
In the statement he made the minister said that 75 to 80 per cent of the steel mills in


the United States would be tributary to this development of iron ore in Quebec and to our seaway. An effort is being made to divert these great iron ore deposits largely for the benefit of the United States. Nothing is being done to build up a steel industry in Nova Scotia. I think it is the duty of the minister and the government, at a time when steel is so greatly needed, to enlarge the present steel plant there or build supplementary industries. That must be done if we are to take our proper place in the development of Canada. At page 1576 of Hansard for December 4 the minister said in reference to this iron ore:
The problem thus is one of a growing gap between supplies and requirements. This gap can be filled partly with imported ore from Quebec-Labrador . . .
Further on he had this to say:
The new ore traffic. Completion of the seaway would change this picture completely. Quebec-Labrador ores, after paying any likely toll, would be enabled to compete in most of the lake districts at current prices for ore.
It is all for the development of that part of Canada and the United States, and there is nothing whatever for the people of Nova Scotia or other parts of eastern Canada. Further on he had this to say:
These facilities make available a plentiful supply of iron ore at a low cost, on which were based the great steel centres of today. Now that production of those ores has reached its limit and costs threaten to increase sharply, the new facilities will make available new and expansible supplies at comparatively low cost.
I could quote more of what the minister said, but what I want to point out is that his whole interest is in providing for development in central Canada and the United States. He does not utter a word to give any indication of assistance to Nova Scotia or eastern Canada generally. In putting forward these observations, I want to repeat that I am not opposed to the development of the St. Lawrence waterway and power project, but I want some statement from the minister and the government on what is proposed for the building up of Nova Scotia and eastern Canada. Some encouragement was in the statement of the leader of the opposition which was quoted the other day by my desk-mate, the hon. member for Royal. I should like to quote it again. It is to be found at page 1465 of Hansard for December 6, and reads as follows:
We have mills on the Atlantic seaboard today. As we plan for the use of iron ore, let us make sure that those mills now existing in eastern Canada are supplied with iron ore on a scale which will require much greater milling capacity than they have today. And let us recognize that while there are immense advantages in carrying iron ore to the established mills in the central part of Canada, there are equally great advantages in assuring steel

supplies at seaports both on the Atlantic and the Pacific, so that we may be shipping steel in the form of steel to our friends and allies in other parts of the world.
That is part of the quotation from the remarks of the leader of the opposition. There is also the question of the development of power. I pointed out a while ago that I think we have a vested interest in power development in central Canada. It constituted a part of the assets when we entered confederation. The minister pointed out that there was a potential of 9 million horsepower involved in the St. Lawrence waterway project. The United States has only 2,900,000 horsepower out of the total of 9 million: 1,800,000 at Niagara and 1,100,000 at the international portion of the St. Lawrence. The total amount developed at the present time is 3 million horsepower in Canada and the United States, leaving a balance of 6 million to be developed.
That means the continued concentration of industry in central Canada, and little is being done to encourage industry in eastern Canada today or in the future. I think the maritime provinces should also be provided with cheap power in order that we may develop our resources and industry. It has been pointed out in the house at different times that we have great power resources in the maritime provinces. About two years ago the possibilities of the St. Mary's-bay of Fundy tidal development were placed before the house, and a reply was made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier). He said he would look into the matter, but that is all I have ever heard of it. He was going to look into it. Two million horsepower are available there. If it were in central Canada it would not only be looked after but the minister would be going up and down the St. Lawrence river to see where it was, whether it could be developed and what could be done for central Canada. He never comes to Nova Scotia to find out. Neither does the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) come down there to look at the power possibilities.

I am sure my hon. friend would not want to make a misstatement. I have been to Nova Scotia many times. I have been to Halifax, Saint John, Charlottetown and several other places. I try to make an annual trip to the maritime provinces but unfortunately it has not been possible for me to do that in the last two years.

I am not saying the minister has not gone to Nova Scotia and the maritimes; it would be a strange thing if he had not. But I say he has never made a personal inspection of the Chignecto canal
St. Lawrence Waterway project. He has never made a personal inspection of the St. Mary's-bay of Fundy power project where it is said that 2 million horsepower can be generate^ on an economic basis.
I doubt whether he has ever visited the Passamaquoddy region where it is possible to develop a million or two million horsepower. He is not interested in these things because they are in the maritime provinces.

I am not going to let my hon. friend make the statement that I am not interested in these projects. That is an unfair statement for him to make. I am sure he does not want to imply that I am not interested in projects in the maritimes, because that is not so. I am stating now that I am.

I am glad the minister is interested. He has made that statement, but I am merely saying that I doubt whether he has ever visited the Chignecto project. I doubt whether he has ever visited the Quoddy project. The cape Split-Minas basin project was referred to yesterday by the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan). We have been told for years and years that millions of horsepower are available there if they can be harnessed, but I do not think any interest has been shown in the harnessing of that power at cape Split. The same applies to Petitcodiac. There are sources of power in that part of the country, and we require cheap power in the maritime provinces. The development of the St. Lawrence project would not be undertaken at this time unless $600 million of Canadian money was being made available for the building of the seaway, thus making possible as a secondary undertaking, almost a primary undertaking, the construction of this power development in central Canada.
We also have great power resources that could be made available as the result of the use of coal. Important developments in power from coal are taking place in Nova Scotia at the present time. Electric power can be generated by this means comparatively cheaply. In my own county of Cumberland the Canada Electric Company, a private enterprise, is developing considerable power but it is not in great quantity, and it is not as cheap as it should be. The cost is not comparable with the cost in central Canada. I think that industry should be subsidized in its use of second grade coal. Some assistance should be given by the federal government to aid in securing the low price coal that is available in the seams in my county in order that industry may be developed and in order that steel smelters may be started in the Chignecto canal region.
The same applies to Pictou county. It has large deposits of low quality coal that might
1682	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway be used for the development of great power undertakings. The same thing applies to Cape Breton. In the coal areas there are enormous deposits of splint, I think they call it, or low grade coal which can be used and which is being used at the present time. This low grade coal can be used for the generation of cheap power. We want some encouragement from the minister and from the government to the end that if this development takes place, the funds will be made available in eastern Canada so that we can supply the electric smelters and other big enterprises in Nova Scotia with cheap power, and that the amount will be comparable with that which is being made available for these enormous expenditures in central Canada at this time. So far there is nothing for us. There are great possibilities in Nova Scotia in the way of waterpower projects and the development of coal-electric power.
It is my opinion that, if the minister had the real interests of Nova Scotia at heart, in view of the hundreds of millions of tons of iron ore to be developed in the Quebec and Labrador deposits, the government's policy would be to see that 2 million to 5 million tons of it is refined in the smelters in eastern Canada, by coal or electricity. But no such undertaking has been given to us under this legislation. A menace appears to be facing our present established industries there, as set out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings and my seatmate, the hon. member for Royal. Great misgivings are felt as to the effect of this development in eastern Canada. But no assurance is given that we will in any way have any development in order to assist us, no matter how old, how definite and how important have been our associations with the establishment and development of Canada. I do not believe that it would be out of place for the government to make available $200 million and more in order that there might be' a development of power, the refinement of iron ore, the building up of basic industries and the establishment of refining industries in eastern Canada, to the end that we might share in the development of Canada, as is our right. That is something that is owed to us by the rest of Canada.
As I said earlier in my remarks, members of the house with whom I have talked and others wherever I go in Ontario, in Quebec and in the west tell me that we in eastern Canada have not fared as we should have, and particularly so in Nova Scotia, in view of the contribution we have made. Here is an occasion on which expenditures running into hundreds of millions of dollars are being made to construct a seaway which it


is claimed will develop that part of Canada, build up shipbuilding and so on, and make a great seaway free from the menace of submarines. That could be done in Chig-necto; there would be no menace from submarines there. If the Chignecto canal were built, the naval and commercial shipping could go through it and avoid going along the exposed Atlantic coast. But it never occurs to the minister that he is going to construct the Chignecto canal in order that there may be protection for our shipping and our naval interests at Chignecto.
I do not know that there is much more that I need to say, although there is a great deal that can be said. The minister talked about the expenditure for the seaway. I think that we, as responsible members of parliament, should analyse these figures. The amount of $300 million is mentioned. It is the impression of a great many people-and I am not able to judge as to the amount- that this expenditure will be at least double that sum. Since the house met last night I have taken occasion to look into what has been the experience with regard to the Panama canal.
A review of the last report of the governor of the Panama canal shows that appropriations for canal construction up to July 1, 1921, amounted to $386,910,301, less capital stock of Panama railroad, $7 million, making a net amount of $379,910,301; plus annual payments to the republic of Panama, 1913 to 1920, of $2 million; additional construction funds appropriated July 1, 1921, to July 1,	1950, amounted to another
$223,223,859, making a total appropriation for the canal of $605,134,160.
Then this report sets out these figures, Mr. Chairman, with respect to the compounding of annual interest, something which is not placed before hon. members by the minister. Further, interest on construction funds compounded annually from 1904 to 1920 totals $128,991,063, making a total capital investment of $734,125,223. A review of the operating statement of the canal for the fiscal year 1950 shows that tolls charged to shipping using the canal, including miscellaneous receipts, amounted to $24,810,323. The net appropriation for expenses amounted to $22,557,703-and we have no estimate from the minister as to what the expenses are going to be in the operating of this canal- resulting in a net revenue in 1950 of only $2,252,620. As I said, the capital expenditure for the Panama canal was $734,125,223. The total revenue for the fiscal year 1949-that is the year previous to the one I quoted-was only $534,374. The minister told the house that the St. Lawrence project is going to be

a self-liquidating one. That may be so and I hope it is; but I have my doubts, and we in Nova Scotia will help pay for it. That is the record of the Panama canal that connects world trade in two oceans. We cannot expect a project such as the St. Lawrence waterway, which serves only as an inland medium of transportation, to be any less costly. The tolls will be low because of low cost articles such as coal and wheat.
We are obliged to contribute to this cost, Mr. Chairman. We in our part of Canada are obliged to contribute to the credit that is supplied in order to build this project. I want to repeat, for the third or fourth time, that I am not opposed to this undertaking, but I want some statement at this time as to what is going to be done for the maritimes. I want it from the minister as spokesman for the government; I want it from the government. I do not think he should ask the members from the maritimes to support this undertaking, which will be a menace to the maritimes, without giving us some undertaking or some hope that something is going to be done for the development of the industries and the refinement of steel in the maritime provinces. That is the position we are in. I want to vote for the minister's resolution but I want some statement from him.

Mr. Speaker, as nearly every other province has had quite a number of speakers on this momentous question, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) calls it, I think perhaps we might have a few words on behalf of the province which I have the honour to represent here, namely Prince Edward Island. If I did not say a few words on this occasion it might be thought that, since Prince Edward Island was wiped off the map printed in an advertisement the other day, we were still removed from the map. I saw an interesting cartoon the other day concerning the removal of Prince Edward Island from this map. It was in some of the leading papers in the east, and pictured half a dozen school boys asking their teacher, who was looking at the map contained in the advertisement, where is Prince Edward Island? With a long pointer the teacher was going from one end of the map to the other but could not find it. I am going to try to place the position of this island before the minister.
The resolution before the committee at the moment seems to be a rather peculiar one, although I must say I am not familiar with the drawing of resolutions of this kind. A corporation is to be created called the St. Lawrence seaway authority. The title seems
St. Lawrence Waterway to be rather broad, and this corporation will have absolute authority if the resolution passes in its present form. Mention is made also of the fact that the corporation may borrow amounts not exceeding $300 million. It appears that authority is given to borrow this $300 million four or five times for this one project, because the resolution says that amount is not to be exceeded at any one time. Probably the minister will have a different explanation of that sentence, but as I see it the St. Lawrence seaway authority has the power to borrow an amount not to exceed $300 million at any time it so desires.
A great deal has been said, Mr. Chairman, by the hon. members from the maritime provinces. For instance, the hon. member for Cumberland just made a speech in which he dealt with the historical aspect of maritime claims, and I consider he made a good case for the maritime provinces. We have listened also to excellent speeches from the hon. members for Royal and for Annapolis-Kings. I might say that all the speeches made on behalf of the maritime provinces have placed good arguments before the Minister of Transport. I should like to deal with the subject from the point of view of my province, the province of Prince Edward Island.
We all know that agriculture is the basic industry of any country. The province of Prince Edward Island not only equals but excels most provinces in the productivity of the soil. This fact has to be considered when we are appealing not only to the Minister of Transport, but to the government, for consideration. My province has no great industry except the basic industry of agriculture. Close to it in importance are our fisheries. In looking at this project from the point of view of an agricultural province, one can see that it is possible we shall not obtain any direct benefit. On the other hand if some benefit can be obtained for the maritime provinces, then perhaps the province of Prince Edward Island can benefit indirectly.
When the minister was introducing this subject the other day he made a wonderful speech in which he stated this was the most important subject upon which he had ever made a statement in this House of Commons. No doubt that is true from the standpoint of the great vision of tremendous benefits that will come to Canada. In his speech, however, I could not detect one ray of hope for any benefit, either directly or indirectly, coming to the province I have the honour to represent. The minister was speaking on behalf of the greatest province in Canada, namely

St. Lawrence Waterway the province of Ontario. He has the honour to represent a constituency lying close to the site of this great project. In view of this fact, he had a right to speak of the scheme in such glowing terms, and to relate what this project would mean to the province of Ontario. I repeat that I followed his speech quite closely, but I could see no ray of hope for the province of Prince Edward Island, the banner province and the cradle of confederation.
If the minister had held out any hope of a plan which would have been of direct benefit to the maritime provinces from which my province might have reaped some indirect benefit, I would have been satisfied. I want to make it clear that I am not opposed to this great project outlined in the resolution before the house. I feel, however, that we should not support it unless we receive some assurance that the maritime provinces will derive direct benefits. The hon. member for Cape Breton South said that he did not care where the government wanted to place steel works for the further processing of steel. I say that we have a steel works now established at Sydney, and that is the type of thing we do want in the maritime provinces. If the minister had announced that he would expand this steel works that is in operation in Cape Breton so that it could manufacture enough steel to supply the demand, that would have met with our approval. Today they cannot fill one-third of their orders. If they want support from the government, let them get it out of this enormous sum that is to be voted following this resolution. I hope that when the minister revises his speech he will give some ray of hope to those of us in the east. I am sure it must have been an oversight on his part, but we want it put in writing this time that we are to get something; that is, if we are expected to support in every way this immense project. Of all the speeches that have been made here, I had great pleasure in listening to the leader of the opposition. In his speech on behalf of this project he included all of Canada from one end to the other. In his remarks he told the house and the minister that the maritimes had been neglected, and they should not be neglected, if this great project is to be what it could be on behalf of the whole of the Dominion of Canada.
I want to say a word or two with regard to my position. I have always said that I am not opposed to it. I know the good people of Prince Edward Island would not desire me to be opposed to anything that is in the interests of Canada as a whole, but they do desire to have something to show for their

support of it. In the maritimes we should have something directly, and it may be indirectly to Prince Edward Island, which we will gladly accept.
As I said on a previous occasion, in reading the speech from the throne I noticed there was one thing which should have applied to our province. When the government said they were going to build this seaway project they left the hope that we in the east, who had been clamouring for different things in our provinces, would now get some consideration. We felt that the government was now loosening up, as it were, and that we could now demand action on some of the projects that we have been talking about over the years but had never received down in the maritimes. I want to mention one in particular. While this project may be a great vision, we all know that from time to time great men in Canada have had great visions. For instance, it was visionary at first when some men thought that the provinces of Canada should become united. That vision became reality. After that the question arose as to where the capital of this Canada of ours would be located. That great man, Sir John A. Macdonald, when looking over the size of the grounds for the capital, had a vision of where the capital buildings should be erected. He had a vision of the greatness of the future of Canada. In talking about the grounds for the parliament buildings, and where they should be erected, he said they should begin at the east of the canal, then run directly in a straight line to what is now Queen street until it meets the river. Had that vision become a reality, instead of the small area we have, all our great buildings in this capital belonging to the dominion government could be in one great common area instead of being scattered around the city.
Another great vision was the linking of eastern Canada with the western provinces by means of a railway. That was finalized, and what a great undertaking it was. There were other great visions. Some became realities and some did not. We have this great vision of a seaway. According to the minister it is going to become a reality, and in the most rapid manner possible. As soon as it is finished it will become the chief competitor of our great railway systems. That may be quite proper. If this project is all that the sponsors say it is, then I believe it could be built and operated from tolls. We all know that the tolls from the canals in Canada today are not sufficient to take care of the burden of running them. Even if it is not a paying proposition, would it not be better for the government to say that the

interest alone on this $2 billion or $3 billion that will eventually be spent would pay the deficit of our railways to the extent of $60 million a year? Would it not be better to put our efforts into the solving of the transportation difficulties of our railways instead of taking on this new project of a seaway for the benefit of centralization in the great provinces of Canada to the detriment of the outlying provinces?
I had hopes when we asked for the development of certain things in our provinces. When we have asked for certain things such as improvements to public buildings, new buildings and improvements in transportation, and also improvement of our harbours, which was at one time the policy of the Liberal party, the reply we received from the ministers was: No money, no material. Yet at the same time they have this enormous surplus, greater than they ever dreamed of getting. They have more now than they ever thought of. They have $640 million in the first half of the year. We find that Prince Edward Island has paid toward that surplus a little over $4,800,000. That is quite a lot of money when you are asking for only a few things that do not cost much over $1,500,000. We have been definitely promised certain things. It reminds me of this. When the Liberal party comes before the people they always have so much to offer but so little to give. This has been very true in our case.
I should like to deal for one moment with a project which, it seems to me, would come within this resolution, because it refers to transportation. I have in mind the harbour improvement we have been promised time and again by all political parties. Only one of those parties, however, has made any attempt to carry out those improvements. That was the Conservative government of Sir Robert Borden.
Here is an opportunity to carry out the St. Lawrence seaway and at the same time help us indirectly through improving our harbours, so that we may ship our products again and so that we may export and import. This may not be important to some who are smiling: I know they have no interest in the matter. But I say to them it is of vital importance to those of us in Prince Edward Island. Let me tell the minister and the committee that for years we have been given definite promises of harbour improvements, but those promises have been passed by.
I believe the promise is set out in one of the Liberal platforms and it was also being stated in the platform of the local Conservative organization, as well as in that of the
St. Lawrence Waterway
federal organization. A plank in the platform of the provincial Liberal administration states this:
We will urge upon the federal government the necessity of improving the Charlottetown harbour and waterfronts, and that the railway marine slip, for which a site has been surveyed, must be built immediately.
We shall also explore new avenues to keep our people employed in the urban centres, and to introduce and develop new industries in our province.
During the last election campaign this was a vital subject, and one to which both major parties were committed. These harbour improvements would mean a great deal to Prince Edward Island and to the city of Charlottetown. We have a good harbour location. It may be that, in common with the harbour at Montreal, Jack Frost occasionally pays a visit so that shipping may be held off for two or three months, or perhaps four or five months, in a year. On the other hand the fact is that we have good harbour facilities and, as the Duncan commission pointed out, we are entitled to have that harbour maintained in proper condition. One of the recommendations by the Duncan commission in 1926 was to that effect.
I hope we will receive some assistance after this resolution is passed, and the seaway is being built. Perhaps I might make some further comments about the indirect benefits that would accrue to Prince Edward Island if an additional plant were added in Sydney, and if perhaps 10,000 more people were employed at that point. This would give us an opportunity to supply foodstuffs to those people, and Prince Edward Island is well suited to do that. We would have a market at home, a market at our own door, for all the foodstuffs we could produce, if we were permitted to supply additional steel works that could be erected in Nova Scotia.
I would repeat that harbour improvements would constitute a direct contribution that could be made for our benefit at the present time. While I do not oppose the resolution, because I know my people would not want me to do so, because of their interest in the Dominion of Canada as a whole, yet as the hon. members for Cumberland, Royal, Annapolis-Kings and Cape Breton South have said, something should be guaranteed directly to the maritime provinces by way of an undertaking as to what will be done for us when this St. Lawrence seaway is accomplished.

Mr. Chairman, I am proud to be a member of parliament in Canada at a time when our country is embarking upon a project of such gigantic proportions and with so much promise as the St. Lawrence seaway development. I believe hon. members

St. Lawrence Waterway from all parts of Canada have taken the Canadian view. While many of them have emphasized the need for improvements in their respective areas, nevertheless this project seems to have been given almost unanimous approval.
As other hon. members have said, the government should bring forth not only a plan for the development of the St. Lawrence seaway, the benefits of which will be reflected chiefly in Ontario and Quebec, but an over-all plan for development in all areas of Canada.
This is a power and transportation project. The minister has said it will enable the rapid development of the Canadian steel industry. It is certain that as a result of it there will be a greater impetus to the industrial development of Ontario and Quebec, and a subsequent increase in the populations of those provinces.
I am sure those of us coming from other parts of Canada would like to see the government undertake other projects which, from our point of view, are as greatly needed as this one, and which would help industrialize the prairies and the maritimes as well as help us increase our populations in those regions.
The St. Lawrence seaway plan has been under study for many years. The government is now bringing forth a measure which will bring about the inauguration of that plan. I am sorry that, thus far, it has failed to announce a much needed project in western Canada, namely the development of the South Saskatchewan river. The far more expensive St. Lawrence seaway project is being embarked upon, but as far as our project is concerned, we are given another commission. We do not know when that commission will report. In fact, I have heard it said that the report cannot be made until the middle of next summer, which will mean that there can be no commencement of that project next year. While we from other parts of Canada support the St. Lawrence seaway project, the fact that the government is bringing forward this large and expensive project at this time leaves the government no excuse for further delay in the development of the South Saskatchewan river project.
It is debatable just what benefits may accrue to western Canada from the St. Lawrence seaway project. It has been implied that the development of this project will result in lower freight rates for grain moving to world markets, which saving would be passed on to the prairie grain growers in the form of increased prices. When considering a statement like that one should bear in mind that grain prices are set at Fort William.

If there is an increase or decrease in the cost of moving grain to Fort William, there is a similar change in the price of grain to the producer. I do not think it follows that a four cent per bushel saving, for example, in shipping wheat past Fort William necessarily means a four cent per bushel increase in the price to western farmers. As a matter of fact I do not think that that result will flow.
If this project results in a substantial lowering of the cost of moving grain from Fort William to the markets of the world, that reduction in cost will be split between the western farmer and the importer of grain. The saving brought about by the St. Lawrence seaway project will benefit the prairie grain producers as well as the buyers of our grain. I do not think it is right to say that a substantial reduction in the cost of moving grain over the lakes means a similar increase in the price received by the western farmer for his grain.
During the last two or three years there has been an increase in the cost of shipping grain on the great lakes. In connection with wheat at any rate that increased cost has been passed on to the buyers of the wheat by adding a six cents per bushel handling charge to wheat obtained under the international wheat agreement. Had this project been in effect during the last two years the saving on the movement of grain over the great lakes and the St. Lawrence river would not have been passed on to the western farmers but would have been passed on to the buyers of our grain. I do think, however, over a period of time the St. Lawrence seaway will result in a saving on freight charges on grain and increased prices to western producers.
If through this measure the government is prepared to assist in the development of the lake ports of Fort William and Port Arthur then I think the government should under an over-all plan assist in the development and further use of Churchill. It is not enough for the government to lay down a plan which benefits in the main two provinces of Canada without at the same time including beneficial measures for other parts of Canada.
On a comparative basis we in Saskatchewan are more in need of power than is Ontario. The province of Ontario has industrialization and rural Ontario is electrified to a large extent. Saskatchewan lacks industries and while some rural electrification is going on, the vast majority of farms still do not have the benefits of electricity. If the farms of Saskatchewan are tc be electrified

we must have new sources of power. Unless the federal government is prepared to proceed with the South Saskatchewan plan the provincial government through its power commission will have to develop its own power site at Fort a la Corne or produce power by the use of coal. The alternative is the development of power at high cost.
The government of Saskatchewan is not at all anxious to embark on the development of new power sources if there is any chance that the federal government will go ahead with the South Saskatchewan plan. Because of the need for power in Saskatchewan, because our province needs industry, because the prairie farmers should have the benefits of electricity the same as the farmers in other parts of Canada, the government should announce immediately that the construction of the South Saskatchewan river project will begin in the spring.
The development of power in Saskatchewan will not represent a dead loss to the federal government. I have here a report on the South Saskatchewan plan over the signatures of L. B. Thomson, director; G. L. MacKenzie, chief engineer, and G. N. Munro, associate chief engineer under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act; A. E. Palmer, superintendent, dominion experimental station, Lethbridge, Alberta, and Dr. C. C. Spence, senior economist, dominion Department of Agriculture, Edmonton, Alberta. This fully-qualified committee states in its report that the annual gross value of commercial energy to be produced from the South Saskatchewan plan would amount to over $2 million.
It is estimated that the South Saskatchewan plan will cost the federal government $68 million as compared to $300 million for the St. Lawrence seaway. When we consider that great benefits will result to the people of Saskatchewan from the South Saskatchewan plan and that there will be revenue derived from that plan, there is no excuse for further delay by the federal government.
I support the St. Lawrence seaway project, as I have said already; but if the government can spend $300 million on the St. Lawrence seaway project I can see no earthly reason why the same government cannot obtain another $68 million for the benefit of the people of Saskatchewan and the prairie provinces generally. I believe the government should give the house an over-all plan for the development not only of the St. Lawrence seaway, which in the main will help Ontario and Quebec, but also a plan for the
St. Lawrence Waterway development of power and the industrialization of other parts of Canada including the prairie provinces and the maritimes.

For a long time I have been advocating in the house and out of it, on behalf of the people in our section of Canada, that a start on the St. Lawrence deep water project should be made. They have a very strong feeling, as is the case in many other parts of the country, that this is a national undertaking which should be completed. During the last session of parliament I brought to the attention of the minister, the government and the house what I thought was a desirable course to follow, namely that we should go it alone. I felt we had lingered on the edge of the precipice of indecision long enough, that there was a limit to the patience of Canada, and that we had reached the position where we should proceed with the waterway as a purely Canadian undertaking.
It is naturally a matter of great satisfaction to me that the government has taken the stand it has and is prepared to introduce legislation to that effect. I have no desire to extend the debate. All I want to say, in what will perhaps be the shortest speech made on the resolution, is that the part of Canada from which I come is strongly and wholeheartedly in favour of the resolution and of proceeding immediately toward the completion of this great national undertaking.

I should like to ask questions of the minister on two different aspects of the St. Lawrence waterway project. The first has to do with shipping. When he spoke on December 4 the minister said, as reported at page 1579 of Hansard:
For one thing, almost half the seaway traffic foreseen is in iron ore.
I had not realized that the shipping of iron ore would constitute such a large proportion of the traffic through the new seaway. That brings up the question as to what ships will be carrying the iron ore. I understand that on the great lakes at the present time iron ore is carried largely in ships belonging to the steel companies. I may be wrong, but that is my understanding. Of course most of that iron ore comes at the present time from-is it the state of Minnesota?
The Mesabi range.
From the Mesabi range, which is in the United States, although I presume the ore from Steep Rock is loaded at Fort William or Port Arthur.
Port Arthur.

I should like to know whether there will be a similar situation with respect
1688	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway to the iron ore from northern Quebec and Labrador. Most of the ore, as the minister has said, is to go to United States steel mills on or adjacent to lake Erie. According to press dispatches, some will also go to United States steel mills on the Atlantic coast. Will the ore be carried in United States bottoms, or is there any restriction under Canadian law by which it must be carried in Canadian ships?

Dealing with the first part of the question as to what ships will carry the iron ore, one must keep in mind the fact that it will be some years before the deep waterway is developed and, as I pointed out in the statement I made, the transportation of the ore will bring into being a new specialized ship which will carry the ore from Seven Islands to the great lakes ports and there take on grain cargoes for the downbound voyage. That is not to say that the present ships will be excluded; the ships operating at the present time on the great lakes, both Canadian and American, carrying iron ore will continue along the same lines. There is a shortage of shipping in that respect at the moment. The ships that will move iron ore from Seven Islands up the lakes will be of a new type in so far as the St. Lawrence is concerned. There are several under construction now.
Where?

Two of them are under
construction now in the great lakes yards. These ships are of a specialized kind.

Is there any restriction on
United States vessels carrying that iron ore from Seven Islands to ports on lake Erie or the Atlantic coast? Are United States ships just as free to carry the iron ore as Canadian ships?

The provisions of the
Canada Shipping Act and of the agreement made between Canada and the United States will apply with respect to that ore as they do with respect to other movements. United States ships are free to come here, but I take it the ships that will take the ore at Seven Islands will be of Canadian registry. Unquestionably those that are being built now are of Canadian registry.
I understand they do not have to be ships of Canadian registry. In other words a ship of United States registry is just as free to carry that iron ore as a Canadian ship. Is that right?

That will be a matter for the mine owner who will be selling his goods to determine. If he cannot charter a Canadian


ship I am sure that is what he will do. If there is a Canadian ship available I am positive that is what he will want, but if there is a shortage of Canadian ships he might seek United States ships. At this time the position is that there is a great shortage of both Canadian and American ships, but by the time the seaway will have been completed I take it there will be sufficient Canadian carriers to transport the ore up the lakes.
May I speak on a question of privilege?
May I finish my questions?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra.

According to the minister's
statement that decision will rest with the mining company. If the mining company wishes to have the iron ore carried by a United States ship the company is free to do so. Am I correct in that belief?
I should not like to leave it on that basis. I would rather put it on the basis that the agreement which exists between Canada and the United States leaves it to the shipper to use either of the two.

I would point out to the minister that the iron ore is being developed largely by United States interests. They control the iron ore. No one can question that fact. It is to be used largely by United States steel mills. I am afraid the minister is being extremely optimistic when he suggests that the mine owners will want to ship this iron ore by Canadian vessels. I hope he is right, but I think he would be far more realistic if he faced the fact that this iron ore is likely to be carried by United States vessels manned by United States crews, and that there will not be a great deal of employment for Canadian vessels, for Canadian shipyards or for Canadian crews. However, I have the answer I was looking for, Mr. Chairman. Before I go on with my other question I should be quite willing at this point to have the hon. member for Simcoe North make the remarks he wants to make.

Mr. Chairman, my colleague really answered the question for the minister. The minister was quite emphatic in saying: that the owners of the mine would surely use Canadian boats to carry the ore. It certainly is a stretch of the imagination, but probably not to the minister when he thinks United States mine owners are going to go out of their way to put their freight on Canadian boats in order to ship it to the United States ports. It is just about in keeping with what the minister said yesterday when he told us-

that the shipbuilding industry on the great lakes would be a great enterprise during a war, in that they would be inland shipbuilding plants.
The minister seems to be satisfied as long as our plants on the great lakes are operating during a war. He made the remark that he could not understand what I was trying to drive at. 1 can quite understand his not understanding when I hear these remarks from him. I was trying to get this government to do something so that our yards would not need a war in order to keep busy. May I remind the minister that the great lakes shipbuilding yards in Canada grew grass on their properties between the first great war and the second great war, and that it took this Liberal government two years to open up the Collingwood yard to build ships, and two and a half years to open up the Midland yard. It required the efforts of the mayor of Midland, of that great paper in the city of Toronto, the Telegram, and of the late member of the house, Dr. Herbert Bruce, to get this government to budge or make any semblance of a move with regard to building ships in yards that for years have been noted for their competence in doing just that, namely building ships of any kind and any type. Yesterday the minister thought he would salve the conscience of the people of Canada by saying that this undertaking will make a great wartime industry. He could not understand what I was trying to drive home to hon. members, namely that we should be thinking of industries that operate during wartime and during peacetime.
Nor can I understand what the hon. member is saying today.

I would not doubt that at all, because you are so convinced that your ideas are right at all times that nobody else could interject any comment in here, and you cannot see the real situation. You are too close to this waterway picture. Step back from it a little bit. Probably you have been in this picture too long.

Mr. Chairman, I thought the hon. member was going to ask a question. I understood that was why he interrupted my hon. friend, and that my hon. friend gave him the floor so he could ask a question; but for the last ten minutes he has been making a speech.
Hear, hear. I am glad you recognize a speech.

Mr. Chairman, before the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra goes on with his questioning I wonder
St. Lawrence Waterway if I might make a few remarks, as a representative of a part of the country which perhaps has a great interest-
Well, Mr. Chairman-
Do you want to speak? I thought you had finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Vancouver-Quadra had the floor, and he may have it if he wants it.

There is one other matter on which I should like to get a statement from the minister. Before I go on to that, may I suggest to the minister that consideration be given to adopting a policy whereby this iron ore will be carried in Canadian ships manned by Canadian crews. I do not believe there could be any objection from the United States to a policy which will ensure that at least the great bulk of this iron ore is carried in our own ships.
The government know they cannot do that.

The other question I should like to ask him also has to do with the iron ore; and I ask it because, as I said a few moments ago, the minister himself has placed such great emphasis on iron ore in this seaway picture. In effect he made it appear that the shipping of iron ore by the waterway was the most important feature in connection with the canal, or in any event one of the prime factors in the whole project. Has the government any plans for a great expansion of Canadian steel production?
No.
I would point out that that is not the minister answering.
That is the right answer, though.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Has the government any plan, for example, for expanding production by the present steel plants in Canada or has it any plan for the erection of steel mills in new centres in this country? I have in mind new sites in the maritimes-for example, in the province of New Brunswick-and in Quebec on the lower St. Lawrence, probably somewhere in the vicinity of Quebec city. Upon my visits to Quebec city I have always felt that great capital has suffered by reason of the development of the city of Montreal. It is tragic to go and see the harbour of Quebec, and note how much shipping could be handled there but how few ships are in the harbour; at least that has been the situation on any occasion I have had the privilege of visiting the city.

St. Lawrence Waterway
Then, are there any plans for steel production in the province of Manitoba? We now have the Steep Rock mine in northwestern Ontario producing large quantities of high-grade iron ore. All of it is being shipped to the United States. I see no reason why that ore could not be used, in part at least, in the province of Manitoba. Are there any plans for the production of steel on the west coast, in the province of British Columbia?
What I have in mind is this. Has the government any plans for using to the maximum our newly discovered and extremely valuable iron ore resources? What
1	have always advocated, of course, is a policy under which the Canadian people get the first opportunity to use their own resources. Hon. members will recall that for several sessions that same issue was fought out in this chamber on the gas and oil pipe-line question. What I should like to know is whether or not there is to be a Canada-first policy with regard to our resources of iron. I do not think anyone has the slightest objection to our surplus iron ore being used by our good neighbours to the south, or by any other nation. So I ask the minister whether or not the government has any plan for the expansion of Canadian steel production.
There would appear to be no such plan in contemplation, Mr. Chairman. In any event, as yet there has been no disclosure of a plan to the house. The main concern seems to be to get this Canadian iron ore down to the United States steel mills. The Minister of Trade and Commerce made that quite clear when he spoke in Washington a few days ago. I should like to quote from a report of his speech advocating the construction of the seaway, which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 29. It ended with this paragraph:
But above all, it would provide the best assurance of adequate supplies of iron ore to feed the steel furnaces of the east coast as well as the great lakes.
The reference, of course, is to the United States. The head of the company which is developing the iron mines in northern Quebec and Labrador is reported as having taken much the same stand. I have here a press clipping from the Ottawa Journal of March 5, 1951, reporting the evidence given by George M. Humphrey, president of the M. A. Hanna Company of Cleveland, Ohio, before the public works committee of the House of Representatives, which committee was considering the St. Lawrence project. It reads:
His company, Humphrey said, plans to ship from
2	million to 4 million tons a year from Seven Islands-


Which of course is on the St. Lawrence river.
-to such eastern ports as Baltimore and Philadelphia, and from there by rail to the furnaces.
I presume that would be to the furnaces on the Atlantic seaboard of the United States. Then the report continues:
The remaining 6 million to 8 million tons would go from Seven Islands up the St. Lawrence to Montreal. From there part would move by rail and part on smaller lake ships to the steel mills.
The reference, of course, is to the steel mills in the lake Erie area. These figures, Mr. Chairman, add up to the 10 million tons of iron ore which is to be the annual maximum produced from the northern Quebec and Labrador mines. Mr. Humphrey, who is head of the company which is mining the ore, said a certain percentage is going to the eastern United States and the remainder to the states south of lake Erie. I am citing that to show that the main concern is to get this Canadian iron ore down to the United States steel mills.
The minister himself, at page 1669 of Hansard for December 6, 1951, made it plain he has the same policy in mind. He was answering questions which had been asked by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and we find these words:
In any event the point was made by the member for Cape Breton South:	Why export Iron ore? I
believe the words he used were these: To whom are we making the iron ore available? Why export iron ore? Well, Mr. Chairman, I do not think I need answer that argument, because the people of this country answered it many years ago. What happened to our gold and our silver in northern Ontario and northern Quebec?
Then the minister went on to try to justify the export of Canadian iron ore to the United States, and he used an argument which I believe is unsound and does not do him justice. I believe it is not a good basis on which to found Canadian policy in this regard. First of all, gold is a commodity itself. It is one of the precious metals, and not in the same category as iron at all. Silver is also a precious metal, and these two metals are sold in the raw state. Any comparison between shipping iron ore to the United States and shipping gold and silver is quite beside the point. I hardly think the minister would push that comparison any further or try to convince any intelligent person that there was much in that argument.
The minister did not stop there, but went on to aluminum. He said: Look at what has happened in the lake St. John area in the province of Quebec, and in the Kitimat area in British Columbia. No one has objected to the shipping out of aluminum, and he compared that with the iron ore. The fact is, Mr. DECEMBER 7. 1951
Chairman, that there again there is no possible comparison. The Canadian contribution to aluminum is electric power, which is perpetual. It goes on and on, and that is the great feature of electric power. We bring in the bauxite from British Guiana-I am not just sure of the source-but both in the case of the development at Arvida and the development at Kitimat practically all the raw material will be brought in from outside Canada. The Canadian contribution to aluminum is the electric power derived from our great water resources. So there again there was not any basis for comparison at all.
The fourth illustration the minister used was copper and nickel. He said the Canadian National is going to build a railway in northern Manitoba, costing many millions of dollars, to take out this copper and nickel which would go to the United States. Well, the minister was far off base on that. The point was carefully considered in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines last session. Evidence was given by Canadian National Railway officials as well as officials of the Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited, the company which is to produce this nickel and copper.
What is happening there is that the Canadian National is building a line into Lynn Lake, where there are these large deposits of copper and nickel; but that copper is to be taken out and smelted at Flin Flon in Canada, and the nickel is to be taken by the Canadian National Railways all the way to Edmonton, there to be smelted in a new plant using natural gas. The bulk of the cost to the Sherritt Gordon Mines Limited is in that plant at Edmonton. I hold in my hand the annual report of this year. It shows that their whole program is to cost $28,318,000, and of that amount $17,522,000 is to be spent for a refinery at Edmonton in Alberta. They have done just exactly the opposite of what Canada is going to do with this iron ore. It is a Canadian development, of the type that will make this country great; not a case of just digging our ore out of the rocks and then shipping it over to the United States for them to refine and sell the products back to us at a vastly increased price.
Then the minister mentioned oil. I do not think he mentioned natural gas, but perhaps we could take the two of them together. He said: "We are going to export our oil to the United States." Well, the government has been very careful to take the position in the house that the oil which is going through the pipe line to Superior, Wisconsin, is not for the United States, that it is to be carried by 94699-108
St. Lawrence Waterway tanker down to Sarnia, Ontario. The government itself has been very careful to keep from getting into the position where it could be accused of sending our oil to the United States. The hon. member for Fraser Valley and I have been busy for a long time fighting out this question in the house, trying to bring about a policy whereby Canadian oil would be shipped to the Canadian Pacific coast before going to the United States. The same applies to natural gas. I think we have a reasonable prospect of winning out and seeing our policy followed; but certainly there is no basis there for comparison with what seems to be the policy of the Canadian government with regard to iron ore.
I submit, Mr. Chairman, that iron ore is in an entirely different position, because iron is not of much use of itself. Iron is the basis for steel, and it is steel which is of such great importance; it is steel which should be produced in Canada. We should be putting the spotlight on the production of steel here rather than on the production of iron ore.
Another thing that worries me about the minister's statement with regard to policy on iron ore is that in his remarks last night he emphasized the great difficulties we would face if we had a Canada-first policy. The hon. member for Cumberland mentioned pulpwood. That was a very hard one for the minister to answer, but he got around it in this way. He said that in pulpwood we have no competition. In pulpwood we can do whatever we like; we can hold up the Americans if we wish; it cannot be compared at all with iron ore, because we cannot do that with iron ore; that there is iron ore away down in Venezuela; if we did not sell them iron ore the Americans would get theirs from Venezuela; that they will not buy ours and we will be in a terrible mess. That was his answer on the question of pulpwood, and I submit to hon. members that on that point, too, the minister was very far from reality.
Then he had another excuse as to why there should be no dominion policy on iron and steel. He said, why, it is up to the provinces; they are the ones who are handling the pulpwood. They fix that up for Canada. They are the only people who can deal with this iron ore. The dominion government cannot do it at all. It has to be done by the provinces. Well, I say the dominion has a few powers left yet. The dominion has absolute control over iron and steel at the moment, and if it wishes to do so it can take steps to see that the very maximum amount of iron ore that can be used in Canada will be used

St. Lawrence Waterway here. This government cannot evade its responsibilities for seeing that Canadians get first chance to use their own iron ore.
Another reason I am worried about the minister's policy, or lack of policy, on this question is that we are going through exactly the same difficulty in British Columbia today. Last year we had the Minister of Fisheries out on the coast. He was questioned about the establishment of a steel industry there. We have been desiring a steel industry on the coast for many years. We thought we had it several times. We have had many promises, but nothing has ever happened. I hold in my hand a clipping from the Vancouver News-Herald, dated November 4, 1950, headed: "Mayhew says time ripe for steel plant in B.C." He is quoted as saying:
"I say a steel industry is a must so far as we are concerned in B.C." he declared Friday.
The article goes on to say:
"This will always be a place where ships are built and steel will be needed for that. There are quite a few miscellaneous industries here now that also need steel."
I am not questioning the genuineness of the Minister of Fisheries. I have great regard for him, and I am not complaining for a moment about his attitude on this question. The dispatch goes on:
"The mill at present uses scrap as raw material." Mr. Mayhew observed.
He is referring to a small mill we have in Vancouver, which does not use raw ore but uses scrap. I continue:
"Steps should be taken, I feel, to develop raw material from the natural ore."
The minister said the ore could be provided from known deposits on Texada island, Zeballos or Quinsam on Vancouver island.
That was last November. What has happened in the meantime. Well, last summer some arrangement was made, in which I think the Canadian government was involved, whereby iron ore from at least two of these districts to which the Minister of Fisheries referred is being sent to Japan. That had to be done through the United States occupation authorities in Japan, and the United States government would have to deal with the Canadian government. But however it was done, the facts are that British Columbia ore is being shipped out to Japan and is being bought back in the shape of steel. I hold in my hand the script of a news round-up of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, dated October 30, 1951, and we find this statement in the script:
Last August the Argonaut Company, a big American firm-
Incidentally in British Columbia this iron ore is being mined by a United States firm.


It is probably a great deal more American even than the firm which is going to mine the iron ore in northern Quebec and Labrador. I continue with the quotation:
Last August the Argonaut Company, a big American firm, shipped its first load of ore out of here from the new Quinsam lake development,-
That was one district referred to by the Minister of Fisheries. The script continues:
-and the Japanese promised that Canada would share in the resulting finished steel.
Today, a good eight weeks sooner than anyone expected, they are making good on their promise.
Down at Ballantyne pier on Vancouver's busy waterfront is the big 10,000-ton freighter S.S. Chuyei Maru.
A Japanese freighter, by the way.

On a point of order, I would ask you to rule, Mr. Chairman, whether a discussion such as this can be brought on when we are discussing jointly two resolutions for the development of navigation and power on the St. Lawrence river. If there is not going to be some control over the discussion we will never be able to come to a conclusion on these resolutions.

The minister himself has
stressed the importance of shipping Canadian iron ore to the United States. That point was discussed in the house last night, and I am speaking about it at this time. I have asked the minister whether the Canadian government has any plan for a great expansion of Canadian steel production, I submit I am entirely in order in pointing out what is being done on the Pacific coast at this time, because it is all part of one policy. The question is: Are Canadians to have the benefit, first, of Canadian iron ore?

The final paragraph of this radio broadcast reads as follows:
The long-necked cranes dipping into her holds are unloading 7,000 tons of high quality steel plate worth one and a half million dollars.
That works out at over $200 a ton for the steel. On the other hand I am told by the experts that Canada would get about $10 a ton for the raw ore shipped to Japan. This is a difference of $190. The situation was summed up admirably in an article headed "The Case for an Iron-and-Steel Plant," written by Mr. C. M. Campbell, one of our outstanding authorities. This appeared in the Western Miner for June, 1951, and states:
Texada, Quinsam, and Zeballos to supply Japan.
Those are the three districts mentioned by the Minister of Fisheries as sources of iron ore.
Published information is that Utah Construction is opening up Texada: that its subsidiary, Argonaut
St. Lawrence Waterway
Mining is opening up Quinsam; and that Frobisher plans to open up Zeballos. The statement is that this ore is to be exported essentially to Japan. The operators will receive about $10 for each ton of contained iron as against a minimum of $120 per ton if made into steel here. We should not be content with holes in the ground and $10, less whatever profit is taken out of the country.
Incidentally the profit goes out of Canada.
We have to go back to the days of Esau to find the record of a similar arrangement.
Again I ask the minister whether the Canadian government has any plan for a great expansion of Canadian steel production. So far as we have been told up to the present time, the plan would appear to be a barefaced exportation of our iron ore in the raw state, without any thought being given to expanding and spreading Canadian steel production. Meantime Canada is crying to the United States all the time for more steel. That is the second question to which I would ask an answer from the minister.
In closing I would like to answer the question asked by the Minister of Public Works. I am in favour of the St. Lawrence waterway development. But I suggest it would have a far greater appeal to parts of the country which will have very little benefit from it if that development included a proper Canadian policy on iron ore and steel.
Finally, I hope the Minister of Transport will give an undertaking that the government will help the maritime provinces. Up to now no such undertaking has been given. Representatives from the maritimes who rise in the house to plead for their people are treated as though they were bad boys, and should not be making so much trouble. Perhaps that is putting it a bit unfairly; but they are being more or less pushed aside, they are just tolerated. They are not given the consideration to which they are entitled.
I wonder what the situation would be if some of those who take this unfair attitude had come from parts of Canada where, year in and year out, the people see their sons and daughters having to leave home and go to what they call Upper Canada-Ontario and Quebec-and in some cases even to British Columbia. When I have visited the maritimes I have had young maritimers inquire from me as to how they might settle in British Columbia. When one has to face that condition, where thousands of young people go to another part of the country while others go to the New England states or to other parts of the United States, he realizes that this is not a laughing matter. Then, when one sees the headquarters of great industrial organizations moving from Halifax to Montreal or Toronto-and I have in mind the headquarters of the Bank of Nova Scotia-

Mr. Chairman, as a representative from Newfoundland I feel I should have something to say about this project which has been looked forward to by the people of Newfoundland as one that will be beneficial to them. As everyone knows, Labrador is an appendage of Newfoundland containing around 110,000 square miles. Until a few years ago it was regarded as being only a source of fish and the site of the operations of the Hudson's Bay Company and Indian trappers. In 1936 the Labrador Mining and Exploration Company was formed to explore the mineral discoveries that had long been reported by geologists. Many people in Newfoundland were most enthusiastic about the possibilities of the iron ore development in Labrador. That was during the days of the commission of government and a large concession of 20,000 square miles was leased to this company for a term of years.
That company is controlled in Canada. I have before me the Financial Post Survey of Mines, 1951, which gives the names of the directors. Mr. Timmins is the president and the company is controlled by the Hol-linger Mining Company .which owns the larger proportion of the stock, and M. A. Hanna and Company, holding the minor interest. This parent company has made agreements with other companies, including the Iron Ore Company of Canada which was formed in Wilmington, Delaware, and which is financed by a group of United States steel companies including Armco Steel Corporation, Hanna Coal and Ore Corporation, National Steel Corporation, Republic Steel Corporation, Wheeling Steel Corporation and the Youngstown Sheet and Tube Company. That company is also associated with Hol-linger Consolidated Gold Mines, Hollinger North Shore Exploration Company and Labrador Mining and Exploration Company. There is also the Hollinger-Hanna Limited, which is a Canadian company formed in 1949 to manage the operations for ten cents per ton. Then there is Hollinger North Shore Exploration Company Limited which was formed in 1942 and which received a number of concessions from the province of Quebec. That company is working in conjunction with Labrador Mining and Exploration Company of Newfoundland because the properties in Quebec and Labrador are contiguous.
I am sure everyone will agree that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra takes second place to nobody in this house in his patriotic desire to see the industries of Canada developed and expanded. At the

same time I am sure he must recognize that even in connection with an industry of which he knows so much, the oil industry, the principal interests are from the United States. We must look to the richest country in the world to provide funds for the development and exploitation of our natural resources. We in Newfoundland must look outside. Before confederation we were told that Canadian capital would pour into Newfoundland to help in the development of that province, but unfortunately that has not been the case. The only capital we have at the present time to develop the industries of Newfoundland- is English and American, with a combination of Canadian and United States capital in connection with this development in Labrador.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra has stressed the desirability of the government promoting the smelting of iron ore in this country. I hope I do not do him an injustice when I say that the hon. member for Cape Breton South seemed to me to favour nationalization, that the government should take over the business if private enterprise is not willing to do it.
I want to correct my hon. friend. I never used the word "nationalization" and I am not responsible for his interpretation.

The hon. member did not use that word, but he suggested-even the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested-that the government should take steps. It would be a great departure from the policy that has been pursued in the past in the development of the great industries of this country if the government should go into industries of that kind. Only the other day the people of England turned out the Labour government because it had gone in for the nationalization of steel. It is certainly very questionable whether the government could do as good a job as private enterprise.
