Mr. Chairman, if what I have to say in connection with the use to which the iron ore is to be put is not relevant, inasmuch as the principal reason for building the waterway is to carry it to the mills, then I do not know what is relevant in this discussion. The minister himself has said that the chief commodity which will be transported through the canals
St. Lawrence Waterway will be iron ore. Therefore I feel it is a matter of very great importance, especially when the question has been so widely discussed by previous speakers, to make a passing reference to it, which is all I intend to do. If I may, I should like to say that we are perhaps looking too far ahead. It will take several years to build the waterway. It will take several years to build the railway and bring the mines to the state where the iron ore can be marketed anywhere.
Furthermore I want to point out-and I believe this is relevant-that we have other iron ore mines in Newfoundland. There is the iron ore mine on Bell island which is owned by the company that operates the coal mines at North Sydney, Sydney and elsewhere in Cape Breton. They are not able to use all the ore that is being produced at Bell island at the present time, and have never been able to do so. Up to the present, time Canada has never been able to use all the ore produced in this country. I would say most of the iron ore produced in Canada is exported somewhere. We export iron ore to Germany, the United States and England.
I should also like to make reference to the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) concerning his desire that Canadian ships should carry the ore to market. May I point out to him that would be a restriction upon the companies operating the mines that might be prejudicial to their interests and might be a burden upon them. They might not be able to meet it. As he pointed out, iron ore sells at a very low price, between $5 and $10 a ton. Therefore in the export of iron ore at so much per ton it might be a matter of great consequence to make a beneficial contract at the best rates possible for transportation. English and Norwegian ships are also engaged in the transportation business to a very large extent. If, as is possible, this valuable high grade ore may be shipped to England, Germany, The Netherlands and places along the Atlantic seaboard, it may be most desirable to have other ships in addition to those of Canadian registry. I doubt very much whether Canadian ships can handle even a small proportion of the production of the mines.
I am sure everyone will agree that it must be a proud occasion for the Minister of Transport, as he told us the other day, to be introducing these resolutions in the house. Coming as he does from the city of Cornwall, where all his life he has looked upon the great restless St. Lawrence passing by his door, some time in the past he must have visualized what is now about to happen. I
1696	HOUSE OF
St. Lawrence Waterway think we can all agree with him it is a matter of pride that he should be the one to introduce these resolutions.
There are two resolutions, one dealing with the development of hydroelectric power concerning which there has not been much criticism. There cannot be any, because it is a natural resource that belongs to the province of Ontario and the state of New York. Its development is not going to cost the dominion a cent. No claim can be made upon the dominion's taxpayers. Therefore it is a natural development which the Ontario government is proceeding with, in the first place for the benefit of the people of Ontario, and I believe indirectly for the benefit of all the people of the dominion. The other feature is the waterway; that is the one that has given rise to the criticism that has come from this side of the house. Naturally I sympathize with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the other speakers from the maritimes who feel that government funds are now going to be invested in a project that seems to hold within it possibilities of damage and even, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, ruin to their coal industry. I am not so pessimistic as he is that the industry cannot stand the shock of further expansion of the transportation system of Canada. No one who has criticized this measure has been so bold as to say that he is opposed to it because it too is a natural development.
Many years ago in the early days of the exploration of Canada les coureurs des bois, French soldiers and missionaries did not hesitate to travel upon the waters of the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa through the rapids for purposes of exploration and to ascertain the resources of the country. It seems to me that in the second half of the twentieth century the government should be criticized if it did not do something to improve the system of waterways beyond its present condition. Anyone who goes to Cornwall today cannot help but feel somewhat astonished at the poor condition of the waterways in that area, and that the proposed development is not only opportune but seems to have been too long delayed. It should have been proceeded with long ago.
When one sees the magnificent locks at Sault Ste. Marie and realizes what has been done in that area, and compares it with the condition existing near Cornwall, one has ground for saying that the Dominion of Canada has been negligent in its duty rather than complimenting it on being ambitious and forward looking. Members from the maritimes have often expressed a certain
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West;. I

criticism of the government that is associated with a feeling of envy of the two central provinces, Ontario and Quebec. It seems to me we have no right to envy these two provinces that have been so graciously endowed by Providence with such marvellous natural advantages and tremendous resources. The St. Lawrence and the waterway system right through to the head of the lakes are a tremendous asset to both these provinces. I cannot see that it is a disadvantage to the rest of the country that industry should be expanded to the extent it has been in Ontario and Quebec, because it means that goods are being produced in this country' that formerly would have been imported from other places. They are being produced in large quantities and are of high quality, thus giving people value comparing favourably with that of the goods they used to import from elsewhere.
When hon. members from the maritimes speak of the decentralization of industry, I wonder what they mean. I feel that what they really mean is that there should be more industries in their home towns. Certainly I can understand every hon. member wishing to see his own home town developed as rapidly and broadly as possible. But, sir, there is such a thing as decentralization even in the central provinces, and it exists today. While I have not a great knowledge of the subject I feel that the little towns and smaller cities in Ontario and Quebec are examples of decentralization. They are not worth an atomic bomb, yet most of them contain industries of considerable proportions and of great value to the people who live there. Decentralization was made possible by the development of hydroelectric power, and I doubt whether in any other area of Canada, or anywhere in the world, electric power has been better developed, preserved so carefully, or so highly thought, of as in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The decentralization that exists in those provinces means that electric power can be supplied to almost all of their villages, towns and cities. There is hardly any point in the two provinces for a long distance from the rivers where the power is developed that electricity is not extensively used.
My hon. friend who has spoken so much about decentralization is no doubt thinking of the industry that exists in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. I feel that is his main objection. He was not thinking of the smaller towns in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec where industries are established. But, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me difficult for the federal government to interfere with expansion of that kind. I have heard my hon. friends on this side of the house speak of the abnormal developments in the city of Toronto.

During the past few years many industries have established themselves there -and millions of dollars, even hundreds of millions, have been invested. But once again we must look at the natural advantages these two cities possess. With their geographical location in the centre of great populations, as they are, they are the natural places for industry to be established.
It seems to me, however, that the government, in developing a waterway like this, even if it is justified in doing it-and I am sure it is-must nevertheless give an ear to the complaints that come from the maritime provinces. They feel that they are being overlooked. My hon. friend who sits opposite me at -the moment, the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, I am sure must be thinking of the great dock in the city of Saint John that is so often empty when it might have shipping there to be repaired or ships being built. I suppose it is the largest dock in Canada; if not, it is one of the largest.
Drydock.

Yes, the drydock. It is -a sad thing that the people of Saint John have to look upon that dock and see it not in use. Many hon. members and many people outside -this chamber often express the opinion that the government should be run like a business. That is a theory with which I have never agreed. I think it is entirely unsound. A government is not a business. In my opinion-, to express the matter in my own simple way, a government should be like a family, and the government should look after those parts of the country which are not so highly endowed with perhaps greater care than those parts like Ontario and Quebec which already have benefited so greatly from the gifts of divine Providence. So if in the maritime provinces, especially in the province of Nova Scotia, there is not the natural resource of water from which electric power can be developed to be sold cheaply, still there are great resources of coal which can be converted into electricity.
In that respect I think the federal government may be able to be of some assistance. If it is found that the development of electricity in Nova Scotia or any other province must be done at a higher cost than when it is produced from the natural resource of water on the St. Lawrence or on the Ottawa, it seems to me there is a case to be made out for a subsidy to those provinces where the electricity cost is so high. In the matter of freight rates the government is doing a similar favour to this province. Perhaps I am not using the right word when I say "favour", but it is showing proper consideration to this province when it adjusts the
St. Lawrence Waterway freight rates so the manufacturers in the maritime provinces can get their products on the market in the central provinces, which have large populations, more or less on the same footing with the manufacturers in the central provinces. In this and in other things, too, I think what is required is for the federal government to be sympathetic.
I know the minister himself is extremely sympathetic to any reasonable argument that is put before him. In conjunction with what others have said I simply want to say a word or two on the question of the development of the great ore bodies in Newfoundland and Quebec. To me it just does not seem right that we should have vast ore bodies in that part of Canada; that Canadians should be engaged to dig that ore, and that Canada

St. Lawrence Waterway should get no other direct benefit from it other than the few dollars we get from digging and transporting it. The minister's arguments for building the seaway would be much more effective if applied to the United States than to Canada. The best of his arguments are that the United States should be building this waterway and not Canada. If Canada is to build this waterway, and if the primary object is to carry the extra tonnage of ore which will result from the mining, then surely some thought should be given to processing that ore in Canada instead of shipping all our raw material 1,500 miles up the waterway to the United States and processing it, and then bringing the processed material back to Canadian mills. That does not seem to be good business even for private enterprise. I certainly would not expect a Liberal government, or a Conservative government either, to undertake this as a government project; but I would expect a Liberal government to be sufficiently interested in the economy of Canada to see that at least whatever private enterprise did process that iron ore was controlled in Canada, and that the iron ore was processed in Canada to the greatest possible extent.
I just received a copy of a speech made by Mr. Crombie, president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association. It is not very often that I quote the Canadian Manufacturers Association, but for once I am in entire agreement with them. He tells us that:
It is expected that during the next five years over two and one-half billion dollars will be spent on the development of our resources.
He goes on to say:
By 1955 we expect to be producing 250,000 barrels of petroleum per day instead of 80,000 . . . 600,000 tons of aluminum a year instead of 400,000 ... 19 million tons of iron ore instead of 3,600,000 . . . and 4,400,000 tons of primary steel instead of 3,700,000 tons.
According to Mr. Crombie we are going to produce 19 million tons of iron ore instead of 3 million tons, but we are going to produce only 4 million tons of primary steel instead of 3,700,000 tons at the present time. He complains of the fact that Canada is exporting most of its raw materials to other countries instead of processing those materials in Canada. Since he is a manufacturer, of course, and interested in manufacturing, I can understand his point of view. But 1 agree with it.
I think we all agree that Canadians should not continue indefinitely to be diggers of canals and carriers of iron ore for the United States or any other country. Canadians should use these natural resources for the development and the benefit of Canada. He goes on to say:
According to the latest available figures, more than half of our farm products are exported as raw 

materials and more than half of our forest products are exported either as raw materials or in a partly manufactured state. It is obviously better for the national economy to export flour rather than wheat, shoes rather than hides, and paper rather than pulpwood. Why should we export wood pulp and import artificial silk?
The more we process our raw materials in Canada, the more we buy Canadian-grown fruits and vegetables, both fresh and processed, the more we buy Canadian magazines, the more we patronize Canadian authors and artists, the more we employ the services of Canadian engineers and contractors, the more employment will be provided in Canada, the more stable and healthy our economy will be, and the higher the standard of living all Canadians will enjoy.
It is with that thought in mind, Mr. Chairman, that I would say the Canadian people are becoming sick and tired of this policy which the government seems to be following, namely that all Canada can do is produce raw materials for export to other countries in order that they may be processed there. I had hoped, as did the hon. member for St. John's West, that when this great discovery was made in Labrador some great benefits would accrue to that part of the country and to Newfoundland, and not just the opportunity to go in there and dig ore for a few dollars a day. Knowing the power resources of the region, knowing there is coal and limestone in the adjacent province of Nova Scotia, I had thought that probably even private enterprise-I did not expect either the government that was then in Newfoundland or the government in Canada would have been farsighted enough to develop that as a publicly owned project for the benefit of the people-would be farsighted enough to see that an industry could be established there where the raw materials are in such close proximity. Instead of that we give foreign capital control of 20,000 square miles of mineral rights. We build 350 miles of railway; we dig a canal up through 110 miles of the international part of the river, and we do it all so that the Americans can get Canadian ore for their plants in the United States, while we Canadians are satisfied with the few crumbs that fall from their table, crumbs in the way of a few dollars for digging the ore and a few dollars for floating it up to the United States mills. I submit that before this project is completed, and while it is still under review, the government should give some consideration to seeing that steps are taken to provide for the people of Canada the greatest possible social benefits that could accrue from an undertaking of this kind.

Why have the maritimes had so many difficulties to face through the years? It is necessary to examine this matter in order to be able to say what the minister and the government will have to do in order to enable the maritimes to take advantage of this and all the other opportunities the minister has referred to. What happened to the maritimes when they came into confederation? In the first place, they were forced to buy goods, which they formerly had bought abroad, at a higher price by reason of the tariffs imposed by Ottawa. This made for an increased cost of production of all the maritime products into the making of which goods from abroad had entered, and thereby destroyed the competitive ability of the maritimes to sell their goods. That is No. 1. All the superficial advantages that you give to

the maritimes which make no allowance for what has happened to the maritimes' economy will be just froth on water.
What was the next thing that happened to the maritimes? They were forced to buy most of their manufactured goods from Ontario and Quebec. They were faced with a long freight haul of one thousand miles on those goods, and with a similar haul for the raw products which they desired to sell in Ontario and Quebec. Unless measures are taken to cancel the evil effects of that disadvantage, then once more any superficial advantage to the maritimes will be of no value.
Those two points are' of major economic importance. They are just plain common sense that any fourteen-year-old boy would be able to see. As I go over the tragic story of the maritimes I find that in the relatively long history of this parliament no attempt has been made to compensate them for the disabilities they suffered by reason of those two obvious economic disadvantages.
What was the third disadvantage they had? Before they entered confederation they had their own banks and their own banking policy. As a result they were able to control credit within their own provinces. Very soon after entering into confederation their banks began to have their policies influenced by federal legislation having to do with interest rates and items of that sort. They began to operate under the federal Bank Act. All too soon the banks in Ontario and Quebec began to acquire a controlling interest in the banks of the maritimes. They were thus able to influence credit policy in the maritimes. Imagine a situation where a bank in Toronto has on its board a number of men who have interests in certain manufacturing plants in Ontario. This bank is able to influence the credit policy of a bank in Nova Scotia; and when a company manufacturing products similar to those manufactured in Ontario comes to that bank-

I believe my remarks have established pretty well the position that Social Crediters will have to take unless that difficulty is cleared away. We favour the whistle, but we certainly do not favour paying too much for it in terms of Canadian well-being. If the maritime provinces are going to be injured in any degree beyond what they have suffered since 1867, then Canada is paying too much for the whistle no matter how valuable it is. I hope I have put myself in the clear so far as the chairman is concerned.
I wish to draw one conclusion before leaving this aspect of the question. The time has got to come when the Dominion of Canada as a whole, and particularly Ontario and Quebec, must take in hand the problem of the maritimes. They have got to extend a helping hand to the maritimes to bring them out of difficulties from which no amount of effort on their part can possibly enable them to extricate themselves. There will be those from the maritimes who will want to get up and make a starched front apology for that region and all that is going on there.
I have on my desk reports of commission after commission, the Duncan commission, the Norman Rogers commission and others I can quote, so it would be just as well for these members not to try to make it appear that things are fairly good for the maritimes. Conditions there are certainly not fairly good.
When the time comes for this government to take in hand the matter of providing for the improvement of conditions in the maritimes, they must take into consideration those four factors which I mentioned. If

they do not do so, then all they will be doing will be providing the maritimes with a little bit of relief to keep them alive instead of giving them the nourishing food which they need in order that they may grow into a strong, virile, vigorous part of the Dominion of Canada. In this St. Lawrence seaway project there is no evidence that any such thing is even remotely in the mind of the department which planned the project or that of the government which stood behind the department. Consequently, to try to pretend that this seaway project is going to be of any real economic value whatsoever to the maritimes is simply to be farcical.
I think probably I have said just about enough on that aspect of the whole question. I just want now to say this. The time has come when something ought to be done about this maritime problem. We have had the submissions of commission after commission. I have here submissions from the probably finest authorities in eastern Canada, time after time, showing how long these people have suffered and how earnestly they have pleaded for some consideration; but nothing has been done for them. We now have to decide whether the maritimes are going to become a great and thriving portion of Canada, able to contribute the amount of well-being to Canadians that their resources and the nature of their people enable them to contribute, or whether we are going to pinch them more and more and smother them to the extent that they just simply cannot possibly do their part.
If the minister is prepared to answer the questions asked of him by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, I will take my seat while he does so. The minister says he would much rather answer those questions when the bill comes in. Let me tell the minister something he certainly must know. Just the minute we get on that bill we will be held strictly to order, under the rule of relevancy, on every single clause and phrase; and as a result it will be impossible to discuss this whole problem successfully at all. That is exactly the way it always is when we get into the bill. If the members of this committee want to have an effective discussion and want to find out the facts concerning this whole measure, the place to find out those facts is when the resolution is in the committee stage, as it is now. I am therefore asking the minister to answer right now the questions asked by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. I am not satisfied to have them answered when the bill is before the house.

Is the minister going to answer my question?
St. Lawrence Waterway
No. I have no intention of making any reply at this stage.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Not by any means. The minister in charge of the resolution has flouted a responsible member of this house. He has refused to answer a perfectly reasonable and relevant question.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps I should have risen before and given my opinion as to the various conditions, one might call them, which have been put by hon. members, in certain cases, on their approval of this resolution. The hon. member who has just taken his seat began his remarks by saying that the Social Credit party was supporting this resolution contingent upon the government declaring its policy as to the development of iron ore or the establishment of a steel industry in Canada or something like that. I hope I am not quoting the hon. member's words wrongly. Other members as well have declared themselves in favour of it, but have spent much more time than is generally the practice in discussing problems which, admittedly, are germane to the question before the committee. Discussion of those problems, however, has occupied more of the time of the committee than has discussion of the resolution which I now have before me.
I am just wondering whether we should continue discussing those problems. On the government side hon. members have said they are not admitting that this resolution and the project that will emerge therefrom will create the injury which is seen by members on the other side. The matter that has been discussed is relevant, but at this time should we not focus the discussion merely on this one point? It has been said: Let us not have any more discussion on the deep waterway but let us have from the minister a statement of policy on iron ore, or on protecting the maritimes as far as the effects of this project are concerned. I understand that this is a difficult question, and I should like hon. members to think over what I have just said. What we have before us is this:
That it is expedient, for the purpose of providing a deep waterway between Montreal and lake Erie, to create a corporation to be called "The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority" with power, inter alia, to expropriate: to construct, maintain and operate all necessary works: to borrow amounts not exceeding three hundred million dollars; to establish tariffs of tolls and to employ such officers and employees as may be required for the purposes of the authority.
That is all I have before me. As was said, latitude is given. In replying to some of the arguments brought forward by some hon.

St. Lawrence Waterway members the minister had to go into the whole iron ore and steel question, and into other germane questions. I think the debate was wide in its scope, and I think hon. members have had ample opportunity to express their views. But at this point, when the general discussion seems to be almost concluded, I should like hon. members to think over whether they should delay the passing of this resolution merely because they would like to have from the government a statement of policy on a matter which to me is not quite covered by the resolution we have before us.

The minister should have answered that question. When a resolution is in the committee stage it is the duty of the minister to answer questions that are asked him. That is the only opportunity members have of probing into the whole problem.

My understanding is that the resolution is debated for the purpose of going into the general subject matter of the resolution. As it now stands, I have made one general statement which took over forty minutes. Then at the request of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra I made a second statement, which took forty minutes, in reply to the hon. member for Cape Breton South and some others. It is now suggested that I make another reply, the object of which will be to reply to my speech, and we will go on and on interminably. I may be mistaken, Mr. Chairman, but I do not think that is the object of the discussion on the resolution. When we get into the discussion on the bill, where we have the terms of the bill and where many of the questions which have been raised here will be answered, I think that will be the place to discuss the matters that have been taken up here.
My hon. friend says there are questions that were asked and that we will not have an opportunity of getting a reply to them because we will be held strictly to the section under consideration. But that is not the position when we get to second reading. As my hon. friend knows, when we get to second reading there is a general discussion on the first section. I will then take the opportunity to reply to the questions that were asked of me by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the other questions that remain unanswered; then I will try to answer them to the best of my ability.

When we get to the second reading stage of the bill it will not be within the rules for the minister to answer questions the members ask. We are undertaking here and now to commit this nation to an
[The Deputy Chairman.]
expenditure that can well amount to $600 million. Surely the members of this house have a responsibility to the public which they cannot escape, to go into every aspect of this proposition in order to determine whether or not it is expedient. How can I tell whether or not it is expedient to spend all that money on that project unless I can get my question answered? That is the point I believe the minister has to explain away.
If the minister does not see fit to answer that question, I have several more. One of the main arguments advanced for the speedy construction of this project is that it is essential to Canada's defence. Will the minister tell the house some respects in which it is essential to Canada's defence position? Surely that is a reasonable question.

I replied to that question last night when I put on Hansard the statement made by the permanent joint board on defence. This board has examined the project carefully and gave four reasons why it was urgent for defence.

Those were merely general conclusions. The board did not go into details. It appears to me as though the house ought to have some details concerning this matter. It may be argued that this is a matter of defence, and consequently should not be aired on the floor of the house. I ask this question. How in the world can hon. members of this house form any accurate estimate of any proposition if they are unable to obtain details concerning that proposition? It certainly looks to me as though the minister should give more details than have been given to justify the statement that this project is essential to Canada's defence.
As I recall it, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong because I have not had an opportunity of reading his final remarks, we were told that we would be building ships in that secluded and invulnerable area of the great lakes. Do I recall correctly, that we would be building ships up there in time of war? This is how the whole thing looks to a person who stands on his own two feet and tries to do his own thinking, just as his mother and father told him to do when he was sixteen years old. War might come within a year or two, and we cannot possibly get this project completed within five years. After we finish the project, how many years would it take us to establish slips which would enable us to build ships with any success comparable with that of the Clyde shipyards? It would take a long time to do that. Surely if an enemy got sufficient control in Britain to destroy those slips completely we would be in a bad way, even if we had that secluded area in which to build

ships. This is the way it works out to the ordinary person. I am not satisfied with the arguments that this constitutes an invulnerable area in which to build ships.
One more thing which comes to my mind is that I am convinced from the arguments of the maritime provinces that if we spent the money we propose to spend on this project to develop power in the maritime provinces and establish strongholds there, with our tremendous air power, naval power and our control over radar and other modern means of war we certainly could make any area in the St. Lawrence valley invulnerable. Instead of having a lot of enemy submarines prowling around the Gaspe peninsula as we had in world war II, we would have them safely shut out in the Atlantic. That is the common sense way of looking at it. I have to rely on the experts and the minister to answer a lot of questions concerning this matter. Those are questions my people will ask me when I go home. Can the minister go into some detail with respect to that?

I do not propose to go into any further detail than I have. At this stage I do not think I should. I believe the matter of defence measures and defence urgency, in so far as the seaway is concerned, might well be considered when we are in committee of a whole on the bill.

I do not find myself
impressed at all with the minister's attitude in this respect. I am sure the ordinary young man and woman in Canada listening to this debate would consider the minister's reply rather flat after the splendid display of oratory he gave us in connection with the railroads and other problems. It is quite a lot short of what we believe the minister is capable of. I should like to ask the minister this question. If it be so vital in the interests of defence that this seaway be constructed so we can deliver iron ore to United States factories to be processed into steel, why is the United States not manifesting more concern about the building of this project? Why should we take the initiative? Has it not got around to the authorities in the United States that they need ore and steel? Cannot the congressmen be impressed with the need?

The United States have manifested great concern over it. The position of the President of the United States is indicative of that, when he states that he is willing, if the congress does not act within a reasonable time, to consent to the development of this project in conjunction with us, both as to power and navigation.
In so far as the first part of my hon. friend's question is concerned, if he will only wait
St. Lawrence Waterway until the bill comes before the house he will find the seaway project is self-liquidating. He is going on the assumption that the taxpayer is going to be faced with a tremendous expenditure. In the original statement I made I indicated that it is intended to liquidate the whole project by the imposition of tolls. Not only that, but it is also indicated that those of the present canals which will be taken over will be operated and maintained by the authority, thereby cutting the expenditures on Canadian canals to a substantial extent.
I am not much concerned about the cost of this thing if the need-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
The minister has been
specializing now for the past two years in this kind of obstruction against me. I say if we let him get away with it we will abrogate most of the privileges of the members of this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The hon. member is still out of order in imputing motives to me. An hon. member cannot impute motives to another hon. member, and I had no such motive. I try to lead the house to the best of my ability. When I see the hon. gentleman doing something I think he should not do I tell the chairman that he should be called to order.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder
whether I might get into this for a moment, and without resorting to the rule book either.
Peacemaker.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Temiscouata has taken the word right out of my mouth. I would like to play the role of peacemaker for a moment or two, if I may. The hon. member for Lethbridge knows that no member of this house, and certainly no one from the opposition side of the house,

St. Lawrence Waterway rises to his feet more often in defence of the rights of the members of the opposition than I do. In fact I have a copy of Beauchesne open on my desk, and I could read a citation in defence of the right of the hon. member for Lethbridge, in committee on the resolution, to seek to get all the information he wants before the bill is brought in. I do not think there is any question about that, and I assert it as strongly as I can. However, I could not help but notice, despite the fact that there are some remarks being made back and forth which are a little sharp, that a few moments ago the Minister of Transport did offer to have a discussion on all aspects of this matter when we get into committee of the whole on the bill, after second reading. He specifically said we could do that on clause 1. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra knows that we sometimes have an argument as to what our rights are on clause 1 of a bill. But the Minister of Transport has given what I think should be accepted by the hon. member for Lethbridge as an undertaking that whatever the argument may be sometimes, on this occasion we will have the right, when we get into committee of the whole on the bill on clause 1, to take up and get the answers, if we can, to the questions the hon. member for Lethbridge is asking here.
As I said before, it is well known that I like to see things threshed out in full. I certainly want to see members of the opposition have their full rights, but we had a discussion on this resolution on Tuesday from five o'clock until ten o'clock of that day. We had it all day yesterday and we have had it thus far today. I think it would serve the purpose of the hon. member for Lethbridge, as well as the purpose of the rest of us, if this resolution could get through today and we could see the bill. As a peacemaker I suggest that we let the hon. member for Lethbridge get what information he can between now and 6:15 o'clock, but I would hope that by that time he would be willing to let the resolution go through and the bill come in on the basis of the undertaking given by the Minister of Transport.
What does the other peacemaker say?
I agree.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Has the hon.
member for Lethbridge any comments to make on the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre?

Mr. Chairman, there is
not a doubt in the world that the position taken by the hon. member for Winnipeg


North Centre is the correct one. If we allow the Minister of Public Works to establish the principle that was implicit in what he said he would abrogate 90 per cent of the effectiveness of the members of the opposition in the house. There is just no answer to that statement.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The point that now seems to be rather important is the one made [DOT]by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
I am sorry, I cannot hear you.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Winnipeg North Centre understood that the Minister of Transport gave an undertaking that on clause 1 of the bill there would * be a general discussion, as has been the practice, and intimated that the hon. member for Lethbridge might be satisfied with that undertaking. He then went on to say that we could let the hon. member for Lethbridge get whatever information he could between now and 6.15, and then carry this resolution. I want to know whether that is agreeable to the hon. member.

Mr. Chairman, this is a
rather new thing to me. In the first place, I think the Minister of Public Works made a personal reflection on me for which he had no justification.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps
that point may be cleared up immediately after. What I would like to obtain, if possible, is the impression of the hon. member of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

I am not prepared to
announce that until the Minister of Public Works rises in his place and makes a statement that he is not going to say that kind of thing any more.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Really, Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman insists and lets this resolution pass I can make a good many promises to him.
On the point of order-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
We have a point
of order before us; we cannot have two at the same time.

On the point of order, is the minister not himself out of order in saying someone is obstructing? If you refer to Beauchesne, citation 299, you will find that is one of the expressions which is objectionable and must be withdrawn at any time. More than that, Mr. Chairman, I certainly

would say that anyone was always out of order who tried to prevent any debate on the maritime provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Perhaps I might
as well comment on the point of order which was raised by the Minister of Public Works. He cited citation 293, paragraph 1, of Beau-chesne. I know that the hon. member for Lethbridge has been insistent, and his insistence might have been construed by other hon. members as being repetitious. Sometimes one does not follow the trend of the questions that are being asked, and it is difficult to perceive whether they are the type of repetition which would justify the application of citation 293 to say that it is obstruction of debate. In his later remarks I think the Minister of Public Works has agreed that, provided the intentions of the hon. member for Lethbridge are good-and he says they are-his point of order will not be taken. On the other hand I think the hon. member for Lethbridge, realizing that the Minister of Public Works has good intentions as well, as he said, will not take umbrage at the remarks made by the Minister of Public Works, and that we can carry on in the few minutes at our disposal and perhaps accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre which apparently has some merit.

Mr. Chairman, I ask the
Minister of Public Works to withdraw the remarks he made.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will withdraw, if it pleases the hon. gentleman.
I want to make this statement. I have never yet obstructed in this house. There are others in this house who perhaps-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. The Minister of Public Works has withdrawn. If he has, the hon. member has no more to say. Shall the resolution carry?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the motion?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I object to this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alphonse Fournier (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me,
on Monday I met the leader of the hon. member's party and the leaders of the other parties, at which time it was agreed that the discussion on the first resolution would apply to the second resolution. Yesterday during the debate I did not bring this matter up, except at the adjournment.
I now feel somewhat ill at ease, because after having these interviews with the leaders it was agreed that this resolution would go through and that the bill would be tabled immediately, so that hon. members would have it. I am appealing to the hon. member to see if we can keep this agreement.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
The information had not been conveyed to me that this arrangement was made by the leader of this group. Since it was made, I am bound by it. Otherwise I would oppose this thing for days, because I believe we are making a very serious mistake in passing these important measures through too fast.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Beaudoin in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: I think some explanation is necessary from the minister. This resolution is completely different from the one just passed, in that it involves an agreement between the province of Ontario and the federal government as to the method of financing. Lands are to be handed over on a reciprocal basis, and so on. I would like the minister to tell us how the financial details are to be worked out as between the province and the dominion.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
Perhaps briefly I might say this: In the first place it was thought unnecessary to introduce a resolution with reference to this agreement at all, by reason of the fact that there is no money passing. Under the terms of the agreement which has already been tabled by the Prime Minister, the province of Ontario is going to establish and produce its share of the 2,200,000 horsepower. But because of the fact that in this agreement there is a clause which provides for the turning over to the province of certain crown lands of the dominion, such as Sheek island,

St. Lawrence Power Development and other islands in the vicinity of the international rapids section, this was done in order that a point of order might not be raised in case someone thought a constitutional point was involved.
Really both resolutions have been dealt with in the general discussion. I have given the only reason for this resolution. That is why the leader of the house thought he had an understanding that both would be considered together.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: That does not answer the question. I have read the agreement. The reason I am asking the question is that, even after reading it, I am still not clear as to the financial responsibility between the dominion and Ontario, and as to the value of the lands. Ontario will be passing some lands to the dominion government and the dominion government will be transferring crown lands to the province. Considerable capital is involved in the transaction, and I do not think the agreement makes it quite clear.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: The agreement certainly makes clear the question of the cost, in so far as the development of power is concerned. In so far as the lands are concerned, those will be determined when the authority in the state of New York and that in the province of Ontario, through the Hydro Electric Power Commission, have completed their negotiations.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: The authority we set up under the first resolution will have complete power in working out the details of this power agreement?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: No, we have nothing to do with that. We have complete power with reference to the seaway.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext: That is why I am asking the questions. Of course right now there is no authority at all, except the agreement on paper between the dominion government and the province of Ontario. Then the state of New York enters into it. Actually there is no supervisory authority so far as the federal government is concerned. Is the province of Ontario going ahead with the state of New York, on its own, so far as development is concerned, without any control at all on the part of the federal government?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE POWER DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT BETWEEN FEDERAL AND ONTARIO GOVERNMENTS
speechtext:
If it is to be an all-Canadian project the answer would be yes. The application would be made by the province of Ontario and the state of New York to a federal body, the international joint commission. But if it is to be a project under the 1941 agreement, then the answer to my hon. friend's question is no.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in.
Mr. Chevrier thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 34, respecting construction of works for the generation of electrical power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
